entries.meaning: Names the party a benefit, a right, or a liability is piling up for. Its home is the paragraph of a contract that says who ends up better off.
examples: All royalties accruing to the estate are paid quarterly.
The tax credit accruing to first-time buyers expires in December.
Interest accruing to the account is posted on the last business day.
The report tallies the savings accruing to the city under the new contract.
Any advantage accruing to the incumbent is small and getting smaller.
Benefits accruing to whoever holds the policy pass to the heirs.

senses.head: Rights and benefits building up to a holder
body: The legal use, usually with under naming the instrument.

senses.head: Interest, dividends, and other money accumulating
body: The accounting use.
examples: All royalties accruing to the estate are paid quarterly.
The tax credit accruing to first-time buyers expires in December.
Interest accruing to the account is posted on the last business day.
The report tallies the savings accruing to the city under the new contract.
Any advantage accruing to the incumbent is small and getting smaller.
Benefits accruing to whoever holds the policy pass to the heirs.

entries.русский: начисляемый в пользу — юр./фин. о правах и доходах, накапливающихся у названной стороны
entries.register: formal; legal, financial, and actuarial. An American meets it in a trust instrument, a royalty statement, or a municipal bond prospectus.
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the party a benefit lands on, or a wh-nominal (accruing to whoever holds the policy) — never a finite clause (✗ accruing to the estate owns the mineral rights). The to is a preposition, not an infinitive marker, so a verb after it must be a gerund: ✗ accruing to receive interest, and in practice the object is a person or an entity rather than an action at all.
entries.pattern: [benefit] accruing to [party] · the rights accruing to [party] under [instrument]
entries.contrast: Three words send a benefit to somebody and they are not the same. Accruing to says the benefit is building up over time, which is why it takes interest, royalties, and credits; inuring to says the benefit legally lands on a named party, which is why deeds use it; attributable to merely assigns a cause. Keep the preposition apart from the plain verb, which needs a subject (interest accrues at five percent).
entries.see also: inuring to, arising under, arising out of, attributable to, for the benefit of

entries.meaning: The honest-arithmetic word: it announces that a raw number has been reworked, and names the distortion that was taken out.
examples: Adjusting for inflation, a ticket cost more in 1975 than it does now.
Median pay is flat adjusting for overtime.
Adjusting for population, the state ranks fourth in traffic deaths.
The chart shows returns adjusting for fees and taxes.
Adjusting for the extra week in the quarter, sales actually fell.
Adjusting for having closed nine stores, revenue held steady.

senses.head: Recomputing a figure to remove a distorting factor
body: The quantitative use.

senses.head: Making an allowance in a judgment
body: The looser use, close to allowing for.
examples: Adjusting for inflation, a ticket cost more in 1975 than it does now.
Median pay is flat adjusting for overtime.
Adjusting for population, the state ranks fourth in traffic deaths.
The chart shows returns adjusting for fees and taxes.
Adjusting for the extra week in the quarter, sales actually fell.
Adjusting for having closed nine stores, revenue held steady.

entries.русский: с поправкой на — пересчитав цифру так, чтобы искажающий фактор больше не влиял
entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard word of economics, statistics, and data journalism
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (adjusting for having closed nine stores) — never a finite clause (✗ adjusting for prices rose → adjusting for the rise in prices). The for is welded on, and swapping it changes the word entirely: adjust to means get used to (adjusting to the altitude), which is not this.
entries.pattern: Adjusting for [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause], adjusting for [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Three near neighbors do three different jobs to a number. Adjusting for X recomputes the figure so X no longer distorts it; controlling for holds X constant so some other effect can be seen; allowing for merely concedes X in an estimate. Discounting is different again — it throws the item out as not worth counting. The past-participial adjusted for modifies a noun and is the form on the chart label (wages, adjusted for inflation).
entries.see also: controlling for, allowing for, discounting, as measured by, indexed to

entries.meaning: Makes room in a claim for a factor the speaker already knows about. It is the honest hedge of estimates, budgets, and forecasts.
examples: Allowing for inflation, the raise is closer to two percent.
Allowing for traffic, the drive takes an hour and a half.
Allowing for rounding, the two totals match.
The schedule holds, allowing for one weather day.
Even allowing for his inexperience, the mistake was serious.
Allowing for being new to the system, she has picked it up fast.

senses.head: Adjusting a figure for a known factor
body: The quantitative use.

senses.head: Making allowance for a person's circumstances
body: The excusing use, close to considering.
examples: Allowing for inflation, the raise is closer to two percent.
Allowing for traffic, the drive takes an hour and a half.
Allowing for rounding, the two totals match.
The schedule holds, allowing for one weather day.
Even allowing for his inexperience, the mistake was serious.
Allowing for being new to the system, she has picked it up fast.

entries.русский: с учётом, делая скидку на — заранее закладывает известный фактор в оценку
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ allowing for the traffic was heavy → allowing for traffic, or allowing for the fact that traffic was heavy). The for is part of the word: dropping it gives you the plain verb, and allowing the traffic means something else entirely.
entries.pattern: Allowing for [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] allowing for [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Three words adjust a figure and they are not interchangeable. Allowing for X builds X into the estimate and keeps it in view; excluding X takes X out of the arithmetic; discounting X dismisses X as not worth counting. Barring is different again — it names a future spoiler rather than a known factor. Against given, which accepts a premise whole, allowing for concedes only a partial adjustment.
entries.see also: discounting, excluding, depending on, considering, given

entries.meaning: The origin clause of American legal drafting. It ties a claim to the event that produced it without saying how tight the link has to be — which is exactly why courts spend so much time on it.
examples: The policy excludes injuries arising out of the use of a motor vehicle.
Any dispute arising out of this Agreement shall be settled by arbitration.
She sued for damages arising out of the collapse of the walkway.
Costs arising out of the recall exceeded a hundred million dollars.
The board reviewed every complaint arising out of the merger.
Claims arising out of being denied coverage go to the state commission.

senses.head: Growing out of a specified event
body: The insurance and tort use.

senses.head: In the arbitration formula
body: Paired with relating to to cover everything.
examples: The policy excludes injuries arising out of the use of a motor vehicle.
Any dispute arising out of this Agreement shall be settled by arbitration.
She sued for damages arising out of the collapse of the walkway.
Costs arising out of the recall exceeded a hundred million dollars.
The board reviewed every complaint arising out of the merger.
Claims arising out of being denied coverage go to the state commission.

entries.русский: вытекающий из, возникший из — юр. связывает требование с породившим его событием
entries.register: formal and legal; an American meets it in an insurance policy, an arbitration clause, and the first paragraph of a complaint
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (arising out of being denied coverage) — never a finite clause (✗ arising out of he crashed the truck → arising out of the collision). The whole three-word string is fixed: ✗ arising of, ✗ arising out from.
entries.pattern: [claims or disputes] arising out of [event or instrument] · arising out of or relating to [noun phrase] — the standard arbitration formula
entries.contrast: The three phrases that drafters chain together are ranked by breadth, and the ranking is litigated constantly. Arising out of needs a causal origin — the claim grew out of the named thing. Arising under needs the claim to be created by a document or a statute, which is narrower. Relating to needs only a connection, which is the widest of the three and the reason it is always added last. Plain arising from is the same word in ordinary prose; caused by is narrower than all of them.
entries.see also: arising under, relating to, arising from, resulting from, in connection with

entries.meaning: The jurisdictional preposition. It says that the claim exists because some named instrument says it does.
examples: The judicial power extends to all cases arising under this Constitution.
District courts have original jurisdiction of civil actions arising under federal law.
Any claim arising under Section 4 must be filed within one year.
Benefits arising under the plan are not assignable.
Disputes arising under the treaty go to a joint commission.
Rights arising under the earlier lease survived the sale.
entries.русский: возникающий на основании — юр. требование, порождённое названным законом или договором
entries.register: formal and legal; a term of art. An American meets it in Article III of the Constitution, in the federal-question statute, and in the dispute clause of a contract.
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an instrument — a constitution, a statute, a treaty, an agreement, a plan. Never a finite clause, and a gerund is impossible (✗ arising under signing the contract).
entries.pattern: [cases or claims] arising under [instrument]
entries.contrast: Against arising out of, the difference is the source of the claim rather than its subject matter: a claim arises under a contract when the contract itself creates it, and arises out of the contract when it merely grew out of the dealings. In federal practice that distinction decides the courthouse — a case arises under federal law when federal law creates the cause of action, which is what gives a district court federal-question jurisdiction. Pursuant to points at the authority for an act; arising under points at the source of a right.
entries.see also: arising out of, accruing to, inuring to, pursuant to, hereunder

entries.meaning: Frozen from the verb bar, "to block." It sets one obstacle in front of an otherwise confident claim and is overwhelmingly a sentence-opener.
examples: Barring a last-minute appeal, the sale closes Friday.
Barring bad weather, we should be in Denver by six.
The team makes the playoffs barring another injury at quarterback.
Barring a few typos, the manuscript is clean.
Barring the second chapter, I liked the book.
She has the votes, barring something nobody has thought of yet.
Barring being called in to cover a shift, I'm free all weekend.

senses.head: Unless this one thing intervenes
body: The default use, always about the future.

senses.head: With the exception of
body: A weaker, static use, close to apart from.
examples: Barring a last-minute appeal, the sale closes Friday.
Barring bad weather, we should be in Denver by six.
The team makes the playoffs barring another injury at quarterback.
Barring a few typos, the manuscript is clean.
Barring the second chapter, I liked the book.
She has the votes, barring something nobody has thought of yet.
Barring being called in to cover a shift, I'm free all weekend.

entries.русский: если не помешает, если не считать — называет единственное возможное препятствие
entries.register: neutral, faintly bookish
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ barring that the weather holds). Pronoun objects take the objective case: barring him.
entries.pattern: Barring [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] barring [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Barring is hypothetical and forward-looking — it names the one thing that could still spoil a prediction. Excepting and excluding subtract something that actually exists. The bare form bar (bar a miracle) is chiefly British; American English keeps bar only in the fixed phrase bar none.
entries.variants: bar (British; in American English only in bar none)
entries.see also: excepting, excluding, failing, pending, absent

entries.meaning: Subtracts an item from a total or a claim. Any modern sentence that uses it is either quoting an old document or making a joke about one; except for is the living equivalent.
examples: Bating a few errors of arithmetic, the accounts were in order.
The whole estate passed to the widow, bating the mill.
Bating his temper, he was an excellent tenant.
Every witness agreed, bating the clerk.
She was, bating one bad season, the best pitcher in the league.
entries.русский: устар. за вычетом, не считая — юр. и антикварное; живой эквивалент — except for
entries.register: archaic; alive only in legal and antiquarian prose
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause in modern use. Do not write bating that.
entries.pattern: bating [noun phrase] · Bating [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: A dead synonym of excepting and barring. Clipped from abating, from the verb abate, "to subtract." Do not confuse it with baiting (luring) or with bated in with bated breath, which is the same root in a different sense — "restrained."
entries.see also: excepting, saving, barring, wanting

entries.meaning: A pure scheduling word. It fixes the first day of a new arrangement and says nothing about when the arrangement ends.
examples: Beginning Monday, the clinic opens at seven.
Rates increase beginning January 1.
Beginning in the fall, all freshmen live on campus.
The library will close at six beginning next week.
Beginning with the third episode, the show finds its footing.
entries.русский: начиная с — офиц. фиксирует первый день нового порядка, о конце ничего не говорит
entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard word in notices and official announcements
entries.complement: a time expression only — a date, a day, or a prepositional phrase of time (beginning in July, beginning at noon). Never a finite clause, and never an ordinary object (✗ beginning the project in this sense, which is the plain verb).
entries.pattern: Beginning [date], [main clause]. · [main clause] beginning [date].
entries.contrast: Starting is the everyday equivalent and is what Americans say out loud; beginning is the version that gets printed on the sign. As of can look backward as well as forward (as of Tuesday, we had no answer); beginning only looks forward. From needs a matching endpoint or an on to feel complete.
entries.see also: starting, effective, following, pending, as of

entries.meaning: The formal topic preposition: it names what a document, question, or complaint is about.
examples: I have a question concerning the deadline.
The memo says nothing concerning severance.
Concerning your invoice, we never received it.
She wrote to the board concerning the audit.
Rumors concerning the merger have been circulating for weeks.
There is a statute concerning exactly this situation.
entries.русский: относительно, касательно — книжн. называет тему документа или вопроса
entries.register: formal
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or wh-nominal (concerning what happened) — never a finite that-clause. To take a clause you need concerning the fact that, which is worse than starting over.
entries.pattern: concerning [noun phrase] · Concerning [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: Concerning, regarding, respecting, touching, and re all mean "about," but only the first two are still in ordinary use, and concerning is the heavier of those two — it belongs to correspondence and reports. In speech, plain about is almost always the better word. Note that the adjective concerning — "a concerning trend," meaning worrying — is a separate, much newer American usage and is not this word.
entries.see also: regarding, respecting, touching, pertaining to, re, with regard to

entries.meaning: The workhorse of the group, and the only one that has kept a foot in three word classes at once.
examples: Considering her age, she recovered remarkably fast.
The price is fair considering the condition of the roof.
Considering the hour, the crowd was enormous.
Considering that he had two hours' notice, the speech was excellent.
Considering you've never done this before, that's impressive.
Considering having to learn the software from scratch, she was quick.
The turnout was good, considering.
It went well, considering — nobody walked out.

senses.head: In view of; taking into account
body: With a noun phrase.

senses.head: Seeing that
body: With a full clause, functioning as a conjunction.

senses.head: All things considered
body: Standing alone at the end of a sentence, as an adverb.
examples: Considering her age, she recovered remarkably fast.
The price is fair considering the condition of the roof.
Considering the hour, the crowd was enormous.
Considering that he had two hours' notice, the speech was excellent.
Considering you've never done this before, that's impressive.
Considering having to learn the software from scratch, she was quick.
The turnout was good, considering.
It went well, considering — nobody walked out.

entries.русский: учитывая, принимая во внимание; с придаточным — «ввиду того что»; отдельно — «в общем-то»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: marginal/participial; also a subordinating conjunction with that, and an absolute adverb
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a finite clause with or without that — considering (that) she had never flown before. It is the one word in this file that freely takes a clause in ordinary American English. It can also stand alone with no complement at all: She did well, considering.
entries.pattern: Considering [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Considering (that) [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], considering.
entries.contrast: Against given: both accept a fact and reason from it, but given is clipped and treats the fact as a settled premise, while considering implies weighing and leans toward excusing what follows. Only considering can trail a sentence alone (✗ She did well, given). Do not confuse it with concerning — considering the evidence means in view of it, concerning the evidence means about it.
entries.see also: given, granted, based on, concerning, notwithstanding

entries.meaning: The word that says a confound has been taken out of the picture. It is the most-borrowed phrase in social-science writing, and the most often borrowed without the arithmetic behind it.
examples: Controlling for age, the difference disappears.
The gap narrows but does not close, controlling for education and income.
Controlling for prior convictions, sentences still varied by county.
Even controlling for square footage, the north side is more expensive.
The study found no effect controlling for hours slept.
Controlling for having children, the wage gap is about six percent.
entries.русский: с поправкой на, при контроле — стат. удерживая мешающий фактор постоянным
entries.register: formal; the standard term in statistics and the social and medical sciences, and now common in newspaper explainers
entries.complement: an abstract noun phrase naming a variable (controlling for age), or a gerund naming a condition (controlling for having children) — never a finite clause (✗ controlling for the subjects were older → controlling for age). The for cannot be dropped or swapped: ✗ controlling age is the plain verb and means something else.
entries.pattern: [main clause], controlling for [variable]. · Controlling for [variable], [main clause].
entries.contrast: Adjusting for recomputes the number; controlling for holds a variable steady so a different effect can be isolated; allowing for is the everyday concession and claims no method at all. In a methods section controlling for is a promise that a model was fitted, and using it loosely in prose — where no model exists — is a quiet overclaim. Keep it apart from the attributive adjective in a controlling interest, which takes no object.
entries.see also: adjusting for, allowing for, as measured by, discounting, based on

entries.meaning: The arithmetic preposition of everyday speech. It adds or, more often, withholds an item from a running total.
examples: There are nine of us, counting the kids.
Counting tips, she clears about forty thousand.
It's a two-hour drive, not counting traffic.
We've lost three games, not counting the exhibition.
The room sleeps six, not counting the couch.
Counting the garage, the place is nineteen hundred square feet.
It's ninety minutes at that place, not counting waiting for a table.

senses.head: Including in a total
body: Positive, usually about people or money.

senses.head: Excluding from a total
body: The far more common negative, not counting.
examples: There are nine of us, counting the kids.
Counting tips, she clears about forty thousand.
It's a two-hour drive, not counting traffic.
We've lost three games, not counting the exhibition.
The room sleeps six, not counting the couch.
Counting the garage, the place is nineteen hundred square feet.
It's ninety minutes at that place, not counting waiting for a table.

entries.русский: считая, с учётом; чаще в отрицании not counting — «не считая» — разг. при подсчёте
entries.register: informal to neutral; a spoken word
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (not counting waiting for a table) — never a finite clause (✗ not counting that the kids came). Almost always negated: not counting.
entries.pattern: counting [noun phrase] · not counting [noun phrase] · [main clause], not counting [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Counting is the conversational including, and it is restricted to tallies — you can say counting the dog about a headcount, but not counting Chapter 4 about a table of contents. Negative not counting is the spoken excluding.
entries.see also: including, excluding, discounting, included, not counting

entries.meaning: Attaches an age to a thing. It is the standard way English says how old something is without a verb of its own.
examples: A farmhouse dating from 1890 sits at the end of the lane.
The dispute is old, dating from the first survey of the county.
Letters dating from the war years turned up in the attic.
The custom, dating back to the Dutch settlers, is still observed.
Records dating back to 1912 were lost in the flood.
A grudge dating back to high school — ✗ dating back from high school.
entries.русский: датируемый, восходящий к — приписывает предмету возраст без отдельного глагола
entries.register: neutral; history writing, museum labels, real-estate listings, and journalism
entries.complement: a date, a century, or a named period — never a finite clause (✗ dating from the house was built → dating from 1890), never a gerund, and never a person. An event may serve as the period (dating from the war), but a bare duration cannot: ✗ dating from forty years.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] dating from [date] · [noun phrase] dating back to [date]
entries.contrast: Dating from fixes the origin point and looks forward; dating back to starts from now and reaches backward, which is why it suits long or surprising spans (a custom dating back to the Dutch settlers). The blend ✗ dating back from is an error and a common one — pick one direction. Since needs a perfect verb in the main clause, and as of fixes the date a statement speaks from rather than the date a thing began. The plain verb keeps its subject (the house dates from 1890); the participial preposition has none.
entries.variants: dating back to, dating to (compressed, common in headlines)
entries.see also: since, as of, circa, ago, back

entries.meaning: Names the thing that has not been settled yet and that will settle everything else. It is the standard way American English hedges a quantity, a schedule, or a decision.
examples: Depending on the weather, the game starts at six or not at all.
Tickets run $40 to $90, depending on the seat.
Depending on what the lab says, we may operate tonight.
Depending on whether the bill passes, the rate changes in July.
She works from home two or three days, depending on the week.
Depending on how you count, there are eight planets or nine.

senses.head: Determined by; varying with
body: With a noun phrase — the range use.

senses.head: Conditional on the answer to a question
body: With a wh- or whether-nominal.
examples: Depending on the weather, the game starts at six or not at all.
Tickets run $40 to $90, depending on the seat.
Depending on what the lab says, we may operate tonight.
Depending on whether the bill passes, the rate changes in July.
She works from home two or three days, depending on the week.
Depending on how you count, there are eight planets or nine.

entries.русский: в зависимости от — называет ещё не решённое обстоятельство, от которого всё зависит
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a wh-nominal — and the wh-nominal is the everyday form: depending on what he says, depending on whether it rains, depending on how many show up. Never a bare that-clause (✗ depending on that it rains). ✗ Depending of and ✗ depending from are errors; the adjective is dependent on or dependent upon, never dependent of.
entries.pattern: Depending on [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause], depending on [noun phrase or wh-clause].
entries.contrast: Three near neighbors sort by what the object names. Depending on names the variable that will decide the outcome; based on names the evidence a conclusion rests on; according to names the source of a report. So the price varies depending on the season (variable), we chose based on the reviews (evidence), according to the reviews, it's good (source). Keep the preposition apart from the plain verb: the outcome depends on the vote is a verb with a subject, while depending on the vote, we may adjourn has no subject and is a preposition.
entries.see also: based on, allowing for, judging by, according to, regardless of

entries.meaning: Sets something aside on the grounds that it should not count — because it is unreliable, unrepresentative, or interested. It carries an implicit claim, which is why it belongs to persuasion rather than bookkeeping.
examples: Discounting the outliers, the results are consistent.
Discounting his own testimony, there is no evidence at all.
Sales rose eight percent, discounting the effect of the promotion.
Discounting inflation, wages have been flat for a decade.
Even discounting the hype, the device is impressive.
Discounting having played at home all month, the streak still means something.
entries.русский: не принимая в расчёт, сбрасывая со счетов — отбрасывает как ненадёжное или предвзятое
entries.register: neutral to formal; common in analysis and argument
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: Discounting [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] discounting [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Excluding removes an item as a matter of arithmetic; discounting dismisses it as not worth weighing. The difference is judgment: excluding the outliers is a method, discounting the outliers is an argument. Not counting is the casual version of excluding, never of this.
entries.see also: excluding, counting, barring, regardless of

entries.meaning: Historically a participle — the object of the obsolete verb dure, "to last," in an absolute construction (during the king's life once meant "the king's life enduring"). Nothing of that survives in the modern word except its membership in this file.
examples: She called during the meeting.
The power went out twice during the storm.
He worked two jobs during college.
During the strike, the plant produced nothing.
Nobody speaks during the reading.
During the sixties, the town lost half its population.

senses.head: At some point inside a period
body: The event is located somewhere within the span.

senses.head: Throughout a period
body: The event occupies the whole span.
examples: She called during the meeting.
The power went out twice during the storm.
He worked two jobs during college.
During the strike, the plant produced nothing.
Nobody speaks during the reading.
During the sixties, the town lost half its population.

entries.pronunciation note: British keeps the yod: /ˈdjʊərɪŋ/ · DOOR-ing or DUR-ing
entries.русский: во время, в течение — в какой-то момент внутри периода либо на всём его протяжении
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: marginal/participial by origin, now a fully grammaticalized simple preposition
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a period or an event — never a finite clause (✗ during I was there → while I was there), never a gerund (✗ during eating → while eating), and never a measure of duration (✗ during three hours → for three hours).
entries.pattern: during [noun phrase] · During [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: The big one is during vs. for: for answers "how long" and takes a quantity (for two weeks), while during answers "when" and takes a named span (during the strike). for · While is the clause form; throughout insists on the entire span, where during leaves the point inside it vague.
entries.see also: for, pending, following, beginning

entries.meaning: The ceiling word. It states a limit from above and, in the negative, is how American statutes write every maximum they impose.
examples: The court may impose a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars.
A term of imprisonment not exceeding one year is authorized.
Any balance exceeding the credit limit is due immediately.
Winds exceeding seventy miles an hour tore the roof off the arena.
Loads exceeding two tons must use the service entrance.
Deposits exceeding $250,000 are not insured.
entries.русский: превышающий — юр. потолок, почти всегда в отрицании not exceeding «не более»
entries.register: formal; statutes, ordinances, contracts, and specifications, where it is nearly always negated as not exceeding
entries.complement: a quantity — a sum of money, a count, a period, a measurement. Never a finite clause, never a gerund (✗ exceeding running the machine all night), and never a person.
entries.pattern: [quantity noun] not exceeding [amount] · [noun phrase] exceeding [amount]
entries.contrast: Not exceeding sets a ceiling that includes the number named — a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars may be exactly five hundred, where under five hundred may not. In excess of is the same meaning in the phrase most American drafters actually write; over and more than are the plain words and are better anywhere but a statute. Do not confuse it with the archaic adverb exceeding meaning "extremely" (exceeding glad), which takes no object at all. On the boundary: this is not a reduced relative, because it will not expand with which is (✗ a fine which is exceeding five hundred dollars) — only with a simple-present relative, that exceeds.
entries.see also: totaling, in excess of, upward of, shy of, up to

entries.meaning: An older, heavier except. Note that not excepting means the opposite of what learners expect — it does not exclude anyone; it refuses to exclude them.
examples: Everyone signed, not excepting the chairman.
The rule applies to all staff, always excepting the medical team.
Excepting the last chapter, the book is a delight.
All fees are refundable, excepting the deposit.
Every state ratified it, not excepting the two that had sued.
entries.русский: за исключением — книжн., устаревающее; но not excepting значит «не исключая, включая даже»
entries.register: formal and dated; standard only after not and always
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause in modern American English. The old conjunction excepting that is archaic.
entries.pattern: not excepting [noun phrase] · always excepting [noun phrase] · Excepting [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: Plain except is the ordinary word, and using excepting where except would do sounds stilted or legalistic. Between the two live forms, the rule is positional: at the front of a sentence American English requires except for (Except for the ending, the movie is great; ✗ Except the ending, the movie is great), while after the noun either works (everyone except him, everyone except for him). Excepting can front on its own, which is the one thing it still does that except cannot. Excepting otherwise survives in two fixed frames: not excepting (which insists someone is included) and always excepting (a legal reservation). The postposed participle excepted is alive and well.
entries.see also: excepted, excluding, saving, barring, except for

entries.meaning: Subtracts a specified item from a set, a total, or a price. It makes no claim about why.
examples: The fare is $340, excluding taxes and fees.
Excluding weekends, that leaves eleven working days.
Enrollment rose in every division, excluding the law school.
The study covered adults, excluding anyone over eighty.
Excluding the two pilot sites, results were flat.
The job takes four hours, excluding driving out and back.
entries.русский: исключая, без учёта — вычитает названный пункт из набора, суммы или цены
entries.register: neutral; the default in commercial, technical, and statistical writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] excluding [noun phrase] · Excluding [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: The exact opposite of including, and the neutral partner of not counting. Against except for: excluding is arithmetical and unemotional, while except for often implies the exception is remarkable. Exclusive of is the formal contract-drafting version. Against discounting: excluding removes, discounting dismisses.
entries.see also: including, excluded, excepting, discounting, exclusive of

entries.meaning: Introduces the fallback. It names the thing that was supposed to occur and quietly concedes that it might not.
examples: Failing an agreement by Friday, the case goes to trial.
Failing payment within thirty days, the account goes to collections.
Failing any response from the seller, the buyer may cancel.
Ask your supervisor; failing that, put it in writing to HR.
We'll take the early flight, or failing that, drive.
Try the main number, and failing that, email the clerk.

senses.head: If the named thing does not happen
body: With an abstract noun phrase, and always fronted.

senses.head: Failing that
body: The fixed phrase, which carries the word in everyday writing and is the only form most Americans ever use.
examples: Failing an agreement by Friday, the case goes to trial.
Failing payment within thirty days, the account goes to collections.
Failing any response from the seller, the buyer may cancel.
Ask your supervisor; failing that, put it in writing to HR.
We'll take the early flight, or failing that, drive.
Try the main number, and failing that, email the clerk.

entries.русский: за неимением, в случае отсутствия; failing that — «а если нет, то...»
entries.register: formal
entries.complement: noun phrase, typically abstract (an agreement, a payment, a response) or the pronoun that — never a finite clause (✗ failing that they agree → failing agreement).
entries.pattern: Failing [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Failing that, [main clause].
entries.contrast: Failing and barring are mirror images. Barring X means "unless X happens," where X is the obstacle; failing X means "if X does not happen," where X is the thing you were hoping for. Absent and in the absence of are the near-synonyms; failing that is the fixed phrase that carries the whole word in everyday writing.
entries.see also: absent, lacking, barring, pending, wanting

entries.meaning: The billing preposition. It attaches the name that is supposed to sell the ticket.
examples: A three-night festival featuring forty local bands.
The exhibit, featuring work from the artist's last decade, opens Friday.
She released a single featuring a rapper half her age.
A remodeled kitchen featuring granite counters and a farmhouse sink.
The network ran a documentary featuring interviews with survivors.
"Empire State of Mind," featuring Alicia Keys — printed feat. on the sleeve.
entries.русский: с участием, в главной роли — афишное «при участии» в анонсах и программках
entries.register: neutral; the standard word of listings, billing, program notes, and marketing copy
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a person, an act, or a component — never a finite clause (✗ featuring the band played twice), and a gerund is clumsy (featuring interviewing survivors → featuring interviews with survivors).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] featuring [noun phrase] · [title] featuring [performer] — abbreviated feat. or ft. on a record sleeve and still read aloud as "featuring"
entries.contrast: Featuring promises that the named thing is a selling point; including merely names a member of a set, and with is neutral about both. Complete with is the ironic cousin — it lists an extra the speaker finds excessive. Involving names a participant while refusing to say what part it played, which is the opposite job. Keep the preposition apart from the plain transitive verb, which keeps its subject (the album features Ella Fitzgerald).
entries.see also: including, involving, complete with, surrounding, with

entries.meaning: The journalist's after. It attaches an event to the trigger that preceded it, and it dangles easily: Following the vote, the room emptied is fine, but Following the vote, applause broke out invites the reading that the applause did the following.
examples: Following a brief recess, the hearing resumed.
Following his release, he moved to Arizona.
Following the storm, half the county was without power.
Three executives resigned following the audit.
The bill was withdrawn following pressure from both parties.
Following that, we adjourned until Thursday.

senses.head: After, in plain sequence
body: No causal claim — the second event simply came later.

senses.head: In the wake of; as a result of
body: The loaded use, and the reason press offices reach for the word.
examples: Following a brief recess, the hearing resumed.
Following his release, he moved to Arizona.
Following the storm, half the county was without power.
Three executives resigned following the audit.
The bill was withdrawn following pressure from both parties.
Following that, we adjourned until Thursday.

entries.русский: вслед за, после — газетное «после», нередко с намёком на причинную связь
entries.register: neutral to formal; heavy in journalism and official statements
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause (✗ following she resigned → after she resigned, or following her resignation). A gerund is grammatical but nearly always clumsy (following being notified → following notification), so the repair for a tempting clause is a nominalization, not an -ing form. The demonstrative pronoun is fine: following that, we adjourned.
entries.pattern: Following [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] following [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: After is the plain word, it can take a clause, and it is almost always better. Following implies the second event came because of the first, which is exactly why press releases prefer it — and exactly why it should be resisted when no such link exists. Subsequent to is worse than either. Do not let it collide with the noun the following (please read the following).
entries.see also: preceding, pending, during, beginning, prior to, subsequent to

entries.meaning: Says you are approaching a number — an age, a clock time, or a length of service — without having reached it.
examples: She's going on forty and still won't fly.
It's going on midnight; we should head back.
He's been at the paper going on twenty years.
The kid is six going on thirty.
They've been engaged going on three years now.
entries.русский: скоро, почти (о возрасте или времени) — разг. «ей скоро сорок», «уже почти полночь»
entries.register: informal, spoken
entries.complement: a number or a number-headed time or age expression — never a clause, never a person or an object (✗ going on the meeting).
entries.pattern: [be] going on [number] · [noun phrase] going on [number]
entries.contrast: Nearly and almost are adverbs and go with anything; going on attaches only to numbers, and only from below — you cannot be going on an age you have already passed. The idiom nine going on thirty-five (a knowing child) is a fixed joke built on the same frame.
entries.see also: ago, back, hence, worth

entries.meaning: The duty-to-consider phrase. In British and international drafting it is how a rule tells a judge or a minister what to weigh before deciding.
examples: Having regard to the age of the defendant, the court suspended the sentence.
The tribunal fixed the award having regard to the conduct of both parties.
Having regard to all the circumstances, the dismissal was unfair.
Having regard to the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the Council has adopted this Regulation.
The trustees must act having regard to the interests of every beneficiary.
Having regard to being a first offense, the panel halved the fine.
entries.русский: с учётом, принимая во внимание — офиц.-юр., брит. и международное; в амер. узусе — given
entries.register: formal and legal, and chiefly British, Commonwealth, and European. An American meets it in a treaty, an arbitral award, an English judgment, and the recital that opens every EU regulation — not in ordinary American prose, where in view of, given, and taking into account do the work.
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (having regard to being a first offense) — never a finite clause (✗ having regard to he was a minor → having regard to his age). Note the singular noun: ✗ having regards to is an error of the same family as ✗ with regards to.
entries.pattern: Having regard to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] having regard to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: It means "taking into account," not "with respect to," and the two blur in careless drafting. With regard to announces a topic; having regard to weighs a factor. Against given, which states a premise flatly, and considering, which weighs and often excuses, having regard to sounds like an instruction to a decision-maker — which is what it usually is, since statutes use it to list the things an official must think about.
entries.see also: given, considering, in view of, with regard to, regarding

entries.meaning: Names one or more members of a set already mentioned, leaving the rest implied.
examples: Several people, including the director, objected.
The package covers five cities, including Nashville.
Everyone was invited, including me.
That's $40, including tax.
The flight takes six hours, including the layover.
All costs, including shipping, are itemized on page two.

senses.head: Naming examples from a larger set
body: The list is partial by definition.

senses.head: Counting an amount into a total
body: Usually money, weight, or time.
examples: Several people, including the director, objected.
The package covers five cities, including Nashville.
Everyone was invited, including me.
That's $40, including tax.
The flight takes six hours, including the layover.
All costs, including shipping, are itemized on page two.

entries.русский: включая, в том числе — называет часть уже упомянутого множества, остальное подразумевая
entries.register: neutral
entries.pronoun objects must be objective: including me, including her and me — ✗ including my wife and I, which is the single most common error made with this word.
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ including that he lied).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], including [noun phrase] · Including [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Postposed counterpart: [noun phrase] included.
entries.contrast: Including opens a partial list; namely and that is introduce a complete one, so including must never be followed by the whole set. Against counting: including works for any set, counting only for tallies. In contracts, including alone can be read as exhaustive, which is why drafters write including but not limited to.
entries.see also: included, excluding, counting, excepting, in addition to

entries.meaning: The successor clause. It carries a right forward to whoever stands in the party's shoes later.
examples: This Agreement is binding upon and inuring to the benefit of the parties' successors.
The covenant runs with the land, inuring to every future owner.
Any refund inuring to the benefit of the estate is divided equally among the heirs.
The policy names a trustee, with the proceeds inuring to the children.
Protections inuring to the employee under the statute cannot be waived by contract.
Savings inuring to the city under the settlement are reported annually.
entries.русский: переходящий к, действующий в пользу — юр. право переходит к правопреемнику стороны
entries.register: legal; deeds, releases, trust instruments, and insurance policies. An American meets it almost only in the closing formula binding upon and inuring to the benefit of the parties and their successors.
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a beneficiary, overwhelmingly inside the frame inuring to the benefit of [party] — never a finite clause, never a gerund (✗ inuring to holding the note).
entries.pattern: [right or benefit] inuring to the benefit of [party] · [noun phrase] inuring to [party]
entries.contrast: In law inure means "to take effect for the benefit of," which is not the inure most Americans know — inured to the cold, meaning hardened by habit — and the collision is why nonlawyers misread the clause as being about endurance. Against accruing to, which is about a benefit building up over time, inuring to is about which party the benefit legally lands on. Older and British documents spell it enuring to.
entries.see also: accruing to, arising under, for the benefit of, in favor of, pursuant to

entries.meaning: The no-blame preposition. It puts a thing in the scene and stops there.
examples: A three-car crash involving a school bus closed the interstate for hours.
The suit is one of several involving the same contractor.
Any incident involving a firearm is reported to the state within a day.
A treatment involving two drugs cut the relapse rate in half.
She took a job involving a great deal of travel.
A rule involving filing twice a year was quietly dropped.

senses.head: Having as a participant
body: The neutral news use, with a concrete object.

senses.head: Requiring; entailing
body: With an abstract object or a gerund.
examples: A three-car crash involving a school bus closed the interstate for hours.
The suit is one of several involving the same contractor.
Any incident involving a firearm is reported to the state within a day.
A treatment involving two drugs cut the relapse rate in half.
She took a job involving a great deal of travel.
A rule involving filing twice a year was quietly dropped.

entries.русский: с участием, связанный с; а также «требующий, влекущий» — нейтрально, без указания вины
entries.register: neutral; heavy in journalism, police and insurance reports, and case description
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (a rule involving filing twice a year) — never a finite clause (✗ an accident involving the truck jackknifed → involving a jackknifed truck).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] involving [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Involving names a participant or an element without saying what part it played, and that studied neutrality is the whole reason reporters and police reach for it: a crash involving a school bus assigns no blame, where a crash caused by a school bus does. Featuring is the opposite — it advertises. Including names a member of a set, and relating to names a topic. Keep the preposition apart from the plain verb, which keeps a subject (the job involves travel), and from the dependent-verb pattern be involved in, which belongs with the dependent verbs.
entries.see also: featuring, including, relating to, surrounding, concerning

entries.meaning: Marks an inference and its evidence in one stroke, and quietly signals that the speaker could be wrong.
examples: Judging by the line outside, the reviews were good.
Judging from her voice, she had been crying.
Judging by what he wrote, he never opened the report.
The house is older than the deed says, judging by the wiring.
Judging by how fast they settled, the evidence was bad.
Judging from two quarters of data, the change is holding.

senses.head: Inferring from physical or documentary evidence
Inferring from a report or a manner
body: Usually with judging from.
examples: Judging by the line outside, the reviews were good.
Judging from her voice, she had been crying.
Judging by what he wrote, he never opened the report.
The house is older than the deed says, judging by the wiring.
Judging by how fast they settled, the evidence was bad.
Judging from two quarters of data, the change is holding.

entries.русский: судя по — одновременно называет вывод и то, на чём он основан
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or wh-nominal (judging by what he wrote, judging by how fast they settled) — never a finite that-clause (✗ judging by he was late). Judging from takes exactly the same complements.
entries.pattern: Judging by [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Judging from [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause], judging by [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: This is the word the traditionalists recommend in place of fronted based on, and the recommendation is worth understanding: nobody expects a judging to have a subject, so the fronted phrase raises no dangling objection even from readers who dislike Based on the data, we canceled. Against according to, which reports what a source said, judging by draws the speaker's own inference from evidence — according to the reviews quotes them, judging by the reviews reasons from them. Judging by and judging from are freely interchangeable in American English; to judge by and to judge from are the stiffer infinitival variants.
entries.variants: judging from, to judge by, to judge from
entries.see also: based on, depending on, given, according to, on the basis of

entries.meaning: States the absence that forced the outcome. Almost always fronted, and almost always followed by a consequence.
examples: Lacking a quorum, the board adjourned.
Lacking any evidence of intent, prosecutors dropped the charge.
Lacking an heir, he left the farm to the county.
Lacking better options, we took the red-eye.
Lacking federal money, the project stalled for a decade.
entries.русский: за неимением, при отсутствии — книжн., почти всегда в начале фразы перед следствием
entries.register: formal to literary
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause, and no gerund (✗ lacking having a quorum).
entries.pattern: Lacking [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: Lacking is the living, slightly literary form; wanting is its archaic twin; absent is what an American lawyer writes; failing is used for an act that was not performed rather than a thing that is not there. Keep the preposition apart from the adjective in the report is lacking in detail, which requires in.
entries.see also: wanting, absent, failing, barring

entries.meaning: The dimension word. It hangs a size on a noun with no verb of its own.
examples: A living room measuring twelve by fourteen feet.
The lot, measuring just under an acre, backs onto the creek.
A crack measuring three inches ran the length of the beam.
They pulled up a trout measuring twenty-two inches.
A parcel measuring forty by sixty centimeters ships at the flat rate.
A tremor measuring 4.1 rattled the windows.
entries.русский: размером в — приписывает существительному габариты без отдельного глагола
entries.register: neutral; specifications, listings, catalog copy, and lab description
entries.complement: a dimension — two or three numbers joined by by, or a single length. Never a finite clause, never a gerund, never a person, and never an ordinary object: ✗ measuring the room in this sense is the plain transitive verb with its subject dropped.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] measuring [number] by [number] · [noun phrase] measuring [length]
entries.contrast: In this frame measuring takes a measure phrase, not an object, and it will not expand with which is (✗ a room which is measuring twelve by fourteen) — only with a simple-present relative, that measures. That is what separates it from a true reduced relative like the report filed on Tuesday, and it is why it belongs in this file. The transitive verb is a different animal and dangles like any live participle: Measuring the room, I found it was short requires the measurer to be the subject.
entries.see also: weighing, numbering, spanning, totaling, by

entries.meaning: A calque of Latin non obstante, "not standing in the way," and still the only common English preposition that is equally comfortable before or after its object.
examples: Notwithstanding the delay, the shipment arrived intact.
She took the job notwithstanding the pay cut.
The objections notwithstanding, the vote proceeded.
His reputation notwithstanding, the jury acquitted him.
Notwithstanding any other provision of this Agreement, Section 9 survives termination.
Notwithstanding that the tenant has cured the default, the landlord retains the right of entry.
Notwithstanding having signed the waiver, she sued anyway.
Every engineer on the project objected; the launch went ahead notwithstanding.

senses.head: Despite (before the object)
body: The ordinary formal use.

senses.head: Despite (after the object)
body: The postpositive use, distinctly literary or legal.

senses.head: The legal override
body: Notwithstanding any other provision — this clause wins over conflicting ones.

senses.head: Cross-class: the bare adverb
body: No object at all, meaning "all the same." The preposition takes an object; the adverb does not.
examples: Notwithstanding the delay, the shipment arrived intact.
She took the job notwithstanding the pay cut.
The objections notwithstanding, the vote proceeded.
His reputation notwithstanding, the jury acquitted him.
Notwithstanding any other provision of this Agreement, Section 9 survives termination.
Notwithstanding that the tenant has cured the default, the landlord retains the right of entry.
Notwithstanding having signed the waiver, she sued anyway.
Every engineer on the project objected; the launch went ahead notwithstanding.

entries.русский: несмотря на — книжн./юр.; единственный предлог, свободно стоящий и после дополнения
entries.register: formal and legal
entries.type: marginal/participial; also postpositive; also a sentence adverb
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund; in legal drafting only, a finite that-clause (notwithstanding that the parties have agreed). In ordinary prose, keep it to a noun phrase.
entries.pattern: notwithstanding [noun phrase] · [noun phrase] notwithstanding (postposed) · Notwithstanding [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: It means despite, but with three properties despite lacks. First, it can follow its object — the objections notwithstanding — which no other concessive preposition in English can do. Second, it heads the override formula that makes one contract or statute clause defeat another. Third, it can drop its object altogether and stand as a sentence adverb meaning "all the same" (He was warned; he went notwithstanding), where despite is impossible. Despite and in spite of are the everyday words, and all three take a noun phrase or a gerund and never a that-clause outside legal drafting: ✗ despite he was tired, ✗ in spite of that it rained → despite being tired, in spite of the rain. Also ✗ notwithstanding of is an error, exactly like ✗ despite of.
entries.see also: given, granted, considering, in spite of, regardless of

entries.meaning: The headcount word, and the standard way a report puts a size on a crowd, a herd, or a workforce.
examples: A crowd numbering about ten thousand filled the square.
Herds numbering in the tens of thousands once crossed this valley.
A staff numbering fewer than twenty runs the whole operation.
Delegations numbering three to five people were seated in front.
Refugees numbering in the hundreds of thousands crossed that winter.
A militia numbering perhaps four hundred held the ridge until dark.
entries.русский: численностью в — «толпа численностью в две тысячи человек»
entries.register: neutral to formal; journalism, official reports, and history writing
entries.complement: a count — a number, a range of numbers, or in the plus a plural (numbering in the thousands). Never a finite clause, never a gerund, and the head noun must be plural or collective: ✗ a delegate numbering one.
entries.pattern: [plural or collective noun] numbering [count] · [noun phrase] numbering in the [thousands]
entries.contrast: Numbering counts heads; totaling adds up amounts, usually money; measuring and weighing take dimensions and mass. All four refuse the progressive relative (✗ a crowd which is numbering ten thousand), which is what keeps them out of the reduced-relative bin. The in the idiom carries a built-in hedge: numbering in the hundreds admits that nobody counted.
entries.see also: totaling, measuring, weighing, spanning, in the neighborhood of

entries.meaning: Assigns a cause, at a slightly elevated pitch. Note that bare owing is an adjective meaning unpaid (the balance owing), a different word from this two-word preposition.
examples: Owing to the weather, all flights are grounded.
The museum closed early owing to a power failure.
Owing to an oversight, your invoice was never sent.
Attendance was down, owing to the strike.
Owing to rising costs, the program was scaled back.
Owing to being short-staffed all summer, the branch cut its hours.
The route was closed owing to the bridge having washed out — ✗ owing to that the bridge washed out.
entries.русский: из-за, вследствие — книжн. указание причины
entries.register: formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause. For a clause use because; owing to the fact that is grammatical but wordy.
entries.pattern: Owing to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] owing to [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The traditional rule pairs it against due to: owing to was the adverbial (Owing to fog, the flight was canceled) and due to the adjectival, licensed only after a linking verb (The cancellation was due to fog). American editors have largely abandoned the distinction and fronted due to is now standard, but conservative style guides still flag it — so owing to remains the safe choice in that position. Because of is safer still and sounds like a human wrote it.
entries.see also: based on, given, due to, because of, thanks to

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French pendant, "hanging." It suspends the main clause until the named event resolves, and it carries a strong implication that the current state is temporary.
examples: The decision is pending review by the board.
She was suspended with pay pending the investigation.
Pending further notice, the office stays closed.
He was held pending trial.
Payments continue pending the outcome of the appeal.
Pending congressional approval, the funds cannot be released.
Two claims are still pending, and the patent is pending as well.

senses.head: Until (an event occurs)
body: The forward-looking sense.

senses.head: While awaiting; during the course of
body: The overlapping sense, common in legal phrases like pending trial and pending appeal.

senses.head: Cross-class: the adjective
body: Meaning "not yet decided," used attributively (a pending case) and postpositively (patent pending). It takes no object, which is the whole test — pending the appeal is the preposition, the appeal is pending is the adjective.
examples: The decision is pending review by the board.
She was suspended with pay pending the investigation.
Pending further notice, the office stays closed.
He was held pending trial.
Payments continue pending the outcome of the appeal.
Pending congressional approval, the funds cannot be released.
Two claims are still pending, and the patent is pending as well.

entries.русский: в ожидании, впредь до — юр.-офиц. приостанавливает положение до исхода названного события
entries.register: formal, legal, and administrative
entries.complement: noun phrase naming an event, decision, or process — never a finite clause (✗ pending the board decides → pending the board's decision), and gerunds are awkward (write pending receipt of the report, not pending receiving the report).
entries.pattern: pending [noun phrase] · Pending [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: Until takes a clause and a point in time; pending takes an event as a noun. The by/until rule sits right next to it and is worth having straight: by names a deadline for a single completed action (file it by Friday), until names how long a state goes on (we're closed until Friday), and pending names the event that will end the state rather than the date (we're closed pending the inspection). Awaiting is the near-synonym but keeps a stronger sense of active waiting. Keep the preposition apart from the adjective pending (a pending case, patent pending), which is postposed and means "not yet decided."
entries.see also: during, failing, following, barring, hence

entries.meaning: Ties a document, a rule, or a record to the matter it belongs to. Its natural home is the filing cabinet, and outside that setting it reads as padding.
examples: Please produce all records pertaining to the settlement.
The statute pertaining to easements was amended in 1998.
Questions pertaining to benefits go to Human Resources.
Pertaining to your second point, the committee has no view.
She testified only pertaining to what she saw that night.
Documents pertaining to hiring before 2015 were destroyed.
The clause relating to arbitration survives termination.

senses.head: Belonging to the subject of; relevant to
body: The legal and archival use.

senses.head: On the topic of
body: The weakened bureaucratic use, where about would do.
examples: Please produce all records pertaining to the settlement.
The statute pertaining to easements was amended in 1998.
Questions pertaining to benefits go to Human Resources.
Pertaining to your second point, the committee has no view.
She testified only pertaining to what she saw that night.
Documents pertaining to hiring before 2015 were destroyed.
The clause relating to arbitration survives termination.

entries.русский: относящийся к, касающийся — канцелярско-архивное; вне бумаг звучит как канцелярит
entries.register: formal; legal, bureaucratic, and archival
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or wh-nominal (pertaining to what was filed) — never a finite that-clause (✗ pertaining to he was hired → pertaining to his hiring). The to is welded on: ✗ pertaining of, ✗ pertaining with, and bare pertaining is not a preposition at all.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] pertaining to [noun phrase] · Pertaining to [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: The heaviest of the topic prepositions. Ranked by weight: plain about is what a person says, regarding is the business default, concerning is a step up, and pertaining to is the top of the scale — it belongs to records requests, statutes, and discovery demands (all documents pertaining to the transaction). Relating to is the same construction one degree lighter and is what most American drafters now write. Against regarding, which merely announces a topic, pertaining to claims that the object belongs to the matter, which is why it survives in law: relevance is exactly what it asserts. Keep it apart from the plain verb pertain, which needs a subject and its own to (the rule pertains to contractors).
entries.variants: appertaining to — the archaic doublet, identical in meaning and now confined to deeds and old statutes, where it survives inside the conveyancing formula the land and all rights appertaining thereto. It is one syllable heavier than pertaining to and adds nothing else; outside a title document it is pastiche. The lighter modern alternative has its own entry: relating to.
entries.see also: relating to, regarding, concerning, respecting, touching, re, with respect to

entries.meaning: Places one event immediately in front of another and asserts nothing about cause — which is the one respect in which it is cleaner than following.
examples: Preceding the vote, the chair read the resolution aloud.
In the week preceding the storm, nobody could buy a generator.
The quarter preceding the recall was the company's best.
Preceding the merger, both firms had already cut staff.
The paragraph preceding this one defines the term.
Preceding that, there had been no complaints at all.

senses.head: Immediately before, in sequence
body: Between two noun phrases.

senses.head: Fronted, opening a clause
body: The formal adverbial use.
examples: Preceding the vote, the chair read the resolution aloud.
In the week preceding the storm, nobody could buy a generator.
The quarter preceding the recall was the company's best.
Preceding the merger, both firms had already cut staff.
The paragraph preceding this one defines the term.
Preceding that, there had been no complaints at all.

entries.русский: предшествующий, перед — офиц. ставит одно событие прямо перед другим, без причинности
entries.register: formal; minutes, reports, and legal recitals
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause (✗ preceding she spoke → preceding her remarks, or plain before she spoke). Gerunds are as clumsy here as after following, and a bare measure of time is impossible: ✗ preceding three days → in the three days preceding the vote.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] preceding [noun phrase] · Preceding [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: The mirror image of following, and it inherits every one of following's problems. Before is the plain word, it takes a clause, and it is almost always the better choice; prior to is stiffer still and worse than either. The live trap is cross-class: the far more common attributive adjective in the preceding paragraph and the preceding year modifies the noun it stands in front of and takes no object, while the preposition sits between two noun phrases and relates them (the year preceding the merger). Most readers meet only the adjective, which is why the preposition reads as officialese.
entries.see also: following, during, pending, beginning, prior to, subsequent to

entries.meaning: The blunt approach-word of American speech. It puts a number just out of reach and hints that reaching it will not be pleasant.
examples: He's pushing sixty and still plays two nights a week.
The truck was pushing ninety when it left the road.
Rent downtown is pushing three thousand a month.
It was pushing midnight by the time we got in.
She's been at that desk pushing thirty years.
The repair bill is pushing what the car is worth.
entries.pronunciation note: PUSH-ing (the vowel of bush, not of hush)
entries.русский: под, почти (о возрасте, скорости, цене) — разг. «ему под шестьдесят»
entries.register: informal; spoken American English
entries.complement: a number — an age, a speed, a price, a clock time, a length of service. Never a finite clause, never a gerund, and never a person or a thing (✗ pushing the deadline in this sense is the plain verb).
entries.pattern: [subject] is pushing [number] · [noun phrase] pushing [number]
entries.contrast: Same frame as going on, and the same one-way restriction: you approach the number from below, and you cannot be pushing an age you have already passed. The difference is attitude — he's pushing sixty is faintly unkind, where going on sixty is neutral, and nearly and almost are adverbs that carry no attitude at all. Keep it apart from the plain verb (pushing the cart) and from pushing it, meaning taking a risk.
entries.see also: going on, upward of, the better part of, shy of, ago

entries.meaning: Announces the subject of the sentence or the document. In American office writing it has almost entirely displaced concerning.
examples: I'm writing regarding your application.
Regarding the budget, we'll take that up in March.
He had nothing to say regarding the settlement.
Please see the attached memo regarding parking.
Regarding what you asked yesterday, the answer is no.
There are new rules regarding overtime.
entries.русский: относительно, по поводу — стандартное деловое «касательно»
entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard business-correspondence word
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or wh-nominal (regarding what you asked) — never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: regarding [noun phrase] · Regarding [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: The trap is the plural. With regard to is correct; ✗ with regards to is an error — regards belongs only in give my regards. As regards (no to) is also correct but stiff. Among the topic words, regarding is the neutral business default, concerning is heavier, respecting is dated, and plain about or on is usually the best of all.
entries.see also: concerning, respecting, touching, pertaining to, speaking of, re, with regard to, as for

entries.meaning: The catch-all of American legal drafting: the phrase that is added last so that nothing falls outside the sentence.
examples: Produce all documents relating to the transaction.
Any dispute arising out of or relating to this Agreement goes to arbitration.
The statute relating to municipal bonds was rewritten in 2009.
She had no information relating to the second break-in.
Costs relating to hiring contractors are billed separately.
Questions relating to what was said at the meeting were ruled out.

senses.head: On the subject of; connected with
body: The drafting use.

senses.head: In the arbitration and discovery formulas
body: Chained after arising out of.
examples: Produce all documents relating to the transaction.
Any dispute arising out of or relating to this Agreement goes to arbitration.
The statute relating to municipal bonds was rewritten in 2009.
She had no information relating to the second break-in.
Costs relating to hiring contractors are billed separately.
Questions relating to what was said at the meeting were ruled out.

entries.русский: относящийся к, связанный с — рабочая лошадка амер. юр. языка, «на всякий случай»
entries.register: neutral to formal; the current American drafting default, and the workhorse of contracts, subpoenas, statutes, and privacy policies
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (relating to hiring contractors), or a wh-nominal (relating to what was said at the meeting) — never a finite that-clause (✗ relating to he was fired → relating to his firing). The to is a preposition, not an infinitive marker, so a verb after it must end in -ing: ✗ relating to hire contractors.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] relating to [noun phrase] · arising out of or relating to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The widest of the topic prepositions, and deliberately so — a demand for documents relating to a subject sweeps in more than one for documents concerning or pertaining to it, which is why the choice is fought over in discovery. Ranked by weight: plain about in speech, regarding in business writing, relating to in drafting, pertaining to in records and statutes. Against arising out of, which demands a causal link, relating to demands only a connection. Keep it apart from the adjective related to (a company related to the buyer) and from the plain verb (the witness related what he saw).
entries.see also: pertaining to, regarding, concerning, arising out of, in relation to, in connection with

entries.meaning: The oldest of the surviving topic prepositions. Use it only when you are quoting or deliberately writing in a legal register.
examples: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion.
The treaty is silent respecting fishing rights.
Respecting the second charge, the defense offered no evidence.
Rules respecting the conduct of members were adopted in 1974.
He would say nothing respecting his sources.
entries.русский: устар./юр. относительно, касательно — старейший из сохранившихся предлогов темы
entries.register: formal and dated; alive in statutes and constitutional text
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: respecting [noun phrase] · Respecting [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: A synonym of concerning and regarding that has fallen out of ordinary use. It survives chiefly because it appears in famous legal language — Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion — where it means "about," not "showing respect for." That collision with the modern verb respect is the reason to avoid it in new prose.
entries.see also: concerning, regarding, touching, re, with respect to

entries.meaning: An old except with a legal afterlife.
examples: All the crew survived, saving the second mate.
Saving your presence, ma'am, the man is a fraud.
Nothing was left standing, saving the chimney.
The order is affirmed, saving the appellant's right to seek review.
Every provision remains in force, saving Section 12.
entries.русский: устар. за исключением, кроме — юр. пережиток старого except
entries.register: archaic; survives in legal drafting and set courtesies
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause in modern use. The old conjunction saving that is archaic.
entries.pattern: saving [noun phrase] · Saving [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: The bare preposition save is the surviving literary form (all save one); saving is one step further back. In law it means "without prejudice to," which is why contracts have a savings clause — saving the rights of third parties preserves those rights rather than excluding them. The two readings, "except" and "preserving," are close enough that modern drafters prefer except for or without prejudice to.
entries.see also: excepting, bating, excepted, barring

entries.meaning: The reach word. It gives a noun a beginning and an end without naming either one.
examples: A career spanning four decades ended with a single email.
The collection, spanning the years 1890 to 1940, was donated intact.
A study spanning eleven countries found the same pattern everywhere.
He wrote a history of the valley spanning three centuries.
Renovations spanning two summers finally finished the roof.
A friendship spanning the whole of their working lives.
entries.русский: охватывающий, протяжённостью в — «карьера длиной в сорок лет»
entries.register: neutral; journalism, obituaries, exhibition copy, and academic description
entries.complement: an extent — a period, a run of years, a set of places or categories. Never a finite clause, never a gerund, and never a single point: ✗ spanning 1975 → spanning the years 1975 to 1980.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] spanning [period] · [noun phrase] spanning [range]
entries.contrast: Spanning needs two implied endpoints, which is why it takes a stretch rather than a date, and why it will not expand with which is (✗ a career which is spanning four decades). Covering is the plainer word and from … to plainer still. The literal, physical sense (a bridge spanning the river) is the same word with its subject restored, and there it is an ordinary participle.
entries.see also: numbering, measuring, weighing, during, throughout

entries.meaning: The pivot of American conversation: it grabs a word someone just said and turns the talk toward it, while pretending the turn was accidental.
examples: Speaking of the weather, did you hear about the storm Friday?
Speaking of money, we never settled the check.
Speaking of your brother, is he still in Denver?
Speaking of being late, where is Dana?
We need a new roof — speaking of which, the estimate came in.
Speaking of Nashville, that reminds me of the last tour.

senses.head: Picking up a topic just mentioned
body: With a noun phrase repeated from the previous turn.

senses.head: Speaking of which
body: With the whole preceding clause as the trigger.
examples: Speaking of the weather, did you hear about the storm Friday?
Speaking of money, we never settled the check.
Speaking of your brother, is he still in Denver?
Speaking of being late, where is Dana?
We need a new roof — speaking of which, the estimate came in.
Speaking of Nashville, that reminds me of the last tour.

entries.русский: кстати о, говоря о — разг. поворот беседы к только что прозвучавшему слову
entries.register: informal to neutral; overwhelmingly spoken
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (speaking of getting there early) — never a finite clause (✗ speaking of he is late → speaking of his being late). One extra restriction no other word in this file has: the object must be something already said or obviously in the air. Speaking of cannot introduce a topic out of nowhere, which is why it is a connector and not just a preposition.
entries.pattern: Speaking of [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Speaking of which, [main clause]. — always fronted, always with a comma.
entries.contrast: As for and as to also switch topics, but they are neutral about whether the topic came up before; speaking of insists that it did, and that insistence is the entire meaning of the word. Regarding announces a subject in writing; speaking of picks one up in conversation, and using it in a memo sounds like a transcript. Talking of is the British counterpart and sounds foreign in American speech. The fixed form speaking of which is what you use when the trigger was the whole preceding clause rather than a nameable thing. Do not confuse any of this with generally speaking, strictly speaking, and roughly speaking, which are sentence adverbs, take no object at all, and are not prepositions.
entries.see also: regarding, concerning, pertaining to, as for, as to

entries.meaning: Fixes the first day of a new state of affairs. Purely temporal — it never takes a person or a thing.
examples: Starting Monday, we're on the new schedule.
The pool is open starting Memorial Day.
Starting at nine, calls go straight to voicemail.
Deliveries run twice a week starting in June.
Starting next semester, the class meets online.
entries.русский: начиная с — разг. соответствие beginning; только о времени, никогда о лице или предмете
entries.register: neutral to informal; the spoken counterpart of beginning
entries.complement: a time expression — a date, a day, a clock time, or a prepositional phrase of time. Never a finite clause, and never an ordinary object in this sense.
entries.pattern: Starting [time], [main clause]. · [main clause] starting [time].
entries.contrast: Starting is what Americans say; beginning is what they print; effective is what the HR notice says; as of is the neutral written form and can also look backward. One redundancy to avoid: starting from Monday — use starting Monday or from Monday on, not both.
entries.see also: beginning, effective, pending, as of
