entries.meaning: The atmosphere word. It gathers everything hanging around an event without naming any of it.
examples: The secrecy surrounding the deal made everyone suspicious.
Questions surrounding his resignation have not gone away.
The controversy surrounding the mural lasted a decade.
Investigators are looking into the circumstances surrounding the fire.
All the publicity surrounding the trial made a jury hard to seat.
The fields surrounding the farmhouse flooded in April — the literal use, and an ordinary participle.

senses.head: Abstract: attending; about
body: With questions, circumstances, controversy, and their relatives.

senses.head: Literal: lying around
body: The ordinary participle, with a concrete head noun.
examples: The secrecy surrounding the deal made everyone suspicious.
Questions surrounding his resignation have not gone away.
The controversy surrounding the mural lasted a decade.
Investigators are looking into the circumstances surrounding the fire.
All the publicity surrounding the trial made a jury hard to seat.
The fields surrounding the farmhouse flooded in April — the literal use, and an ordinary participle.

entries.русский: вокруг, связанный с — «обстоятельства, окружающие происшествие»; букв. «лежащий вокруг»
entries.register: neutral; the standard word of news writing and official inquiry
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an event, a decision, or a person — never a finite clause (✗ the secrecy surrounding he resigned → surrounding his resignation), never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [abstract noun] surrounding [event] · the circumstances surrounding [event]
entries.contrast: In this use nothing physically surrounds anything: the questions surrounding his resignation are questions about it, and that bleaching is what makes the word a preposition rather than a live participle. It is confined to a short list of abstract head nouns — questions, controversy, secrecy, mystery, circumstances, publicity, debate, speculation. Put a concrete noun in front and the literal sense returns (the fields surrounding the farmhouse), and there it is an ordinary participle. The attributive adjective in the surrounding countryside takes no object at all, which is the usual test.
entries.see also: concerning, relating to, involving, about, in the wake of

entries.meaning: The adding-up word. It closes a list of amounts with their sum and no verb.
examples: Fines totaling $2.3 million were levied against the utility.
Grants totaling just over a million dollars went to eleven schools.
He served three sentences totaling eleven years.
Layoffs totaling nine percent of the workforce were announced Monday.
Repairs totaling four thousand dollars were covered by the warranty.
Contributions totaling less than two hundred dollars need not be itemized.
entries.русский: на общую сумму, всего — закрывает перечень цифр их итогом без глагола
entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard word of financial reporting, court filings, and news
entries.complement: an amount — money, a count, a span of time. Never a finite clause, never a gerund, and the head noun must be plural or collective, because a total is a sum of things: ✗ a fine totaling $500 → a fine of $500.
entries.pattern: [plural noun] totaling [amount]
entries.contrast: Totaling sums items already named; numbering counts them; exceeding sets a ceiling over them. Amounting to is the heavier synonym and prefers a single figure with a note of judgment (conduct amounting to fraud). Like the rest of the measure group it refuses the progressive relative (✗ fines which are totaling two million dollars).
entries.variants: totalling (British spelling; American English uses one l)
entries.see also: numbering, exceeding, measuring, in the amount of, in excess of

entries.meaning: Survives almost entirely in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century prose and in deliberate pastiche of it.
examples: Touching the matter of the estate, I have written to counsel.
He was examined touching his knowledge of the conspiracy.
Touching these accusations, the bishop was silent.
Nothing in the record is decisive touching the question of intent.
Touching your late letter, I can add little.
entries.русский: устар. относительно, касательно — только в прозе XVII–XVIII вв. и в стилизациях под неё
entries.register: archaic; ecclesiastical, legal, and literary
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: touching [noun phrase] · Touching [noun phrase], [main clause].
entries.contrast: Another dead synonym of concerning. The living modern word spelled the same way is the adjective (a touching tribute) and the verb (touching the wire), so a modern reader hits touching the matter of the will and stumbles. Use concerning or about.
entries.see also: concerning, respecting, regarding, re

entries.meaning: The older sibling of lacking, from the original sense of want, "to be missing."
examples: Wanting a quorum, the assembly adjourned.
Wanting better evidence, the coroner recorded an open verdict.
Wanting a will, the estate passed to the next of kin.
A hundred wanting three is ninety-seven.
He served forty years wanting two months.
It was a full crew wanting one deckhand.
Wanting any word from headquarters, the captain acted on his own.

senses.head: In the absence of; without
body: The concessive-causal use.

senses.head: Less; minus
body: A subtractive use, now confined to old prose and set arithmetic.
examples: Wanting a quorum, the assembly adjourned.
Wanting better evidence, the coroner recorded an open verdict.
Wanting a will, the estate passed to the next of kin.
A hundred wanting three is ninety-seven.
He served forty years wanting two months.
It was a full crew wanting one deckhand.
Wanting any word from headquarters, the captain acted on his own.

entries.русский: устар./книжн. за неимением, при отсутствии; также «без, минус» при вычитании
entries.register: archaic to formal-literary
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a finite clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: Wanting [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [quantity] wanting [quantity].
entries.contrast: Lacking is the modern equivalent for the first sense; minus or less covers the subtractive second sense. Keep the preposition apart from the predicative adjective in he was found wanting and from the ordinary verb want, "desire," which is the meaning most learners assume and which is never right here.
entries.see also: lacking, failing, absent, bating, minus, less

entries.meaning: The mass word, and the one member of the measure group that most often gets confused with a completely different verb spelled the same way.
examples: A tumor weighing nearly two pounds was removed.
They landed a halibut weighing over a hundred pounds.
Anything weighing more than fifty pounds ships freight.
A calf weighing eighty pounds at birth is unusual.
He carried a pack weighing a third of what he did.
A meteorite fragment weighing eleven grams sold for four thousand dollars.
entries.русский: весом в — «посылка весом в три килограмма»
entries.register: neutral; shipping, medicine, agriculture, and any prose that has to say how heavy something is
entries.complement: a weight — never a finite clause, never a gerund, never a person. The other weighing, meaning "considering," takes a real object (weighing the options) and is a live participle with a subject to match.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] weighing [weight]
entries.contrast: The two weighings split cleanly by complement and by danger. In the measure frame the phrase takes a quantity, cannot passivize, and cannot dangle, because there is no one doing the weighing: a box weighing forty pounds. In the transitive frame it takes an object and must dangle-check like any participle: ✗ Weighing the options, the decision was postponed has the decision doing the weighing. And as in the rest of the measure group, ✗ a box which is weighing forty pounds is impossible — only that weighs.
entries.see also: measuring, numbering, totaling, spanning, exceeding

entries.meaning: Attaches an escort, an enclosure, or a companion symptom to the thing that matters, and quietly ranks the two.
examples: The senator arrived accompanied by two aides and a lawyer.
Applications must be accompanied by a check for the filing fee.
Fever accompanied by a rash should be reported the same day.
The storm was accompanied by winds of sixty miles an hour.
Minors unaccompanied by an adult are not admitted after nine.
She sang the aria accompanied by a single guitar.

senses.head: In the company of
body: With people.

senses.head: Coming with; enclosed with
body: With documents, payments, and paperwork.

senses.head: Occurring together with
body: With symptoms, weather, and other phenomena — and in music, with the instrument behind the singer.
examples: The senator arrived accompanied by two aides and a lawyer.
Applications must be accompanied by a check for the filing fee.
Fever accompanied by a rash should be reported the same day.
The storm was accompanied by winds of sixty miles an hour.
Minors unaccompanied by an adult are not admitted after nine.
She sang the aria accompanied by a single guitar.

entries.русский: в сопровождении, вместе с — о спутниках, приложенных документах, сопутствующих явлениях
entries.register: neutral to formal; notices, rules, travel and admission policies, medical writing, and concert programs
entries.complement: a noun phrase — a person, a document, or a phenomenon. A gerund is grammatical but rare (accompanied by being asked for identification), and a finite clause is impossible (✗ accompanied by his wife came too). A pronoun object is objective: accompanied by me, ✗ accompanied by I.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] accompanied by [noun phrase] · Accompanied by [noun phrase], [main clause]. · unaccompanied by [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The construction keeps a hierarchy: the subject is the main party and the object is the escort, which is why the senator, accompanied by two aides is normal and the reverse sounds absurd. It shares that with along with and together with, and it shares their agreement rule too — the phrase is parenthetical, so the verb still agrees with the first noun (The manager, accompanied by three players, was fined). Plain with is the everyday word and levels the hierarchy. The negative unaccompanied by is the fixed form on rules and forms; ✗ not accompanied by in that slot reads as a mistake.
entries.variants: unaccompanied by (the negative, standard in rules and notices)
entries.see also: along with, together with, complete with, followed by, with

entries.meaning: The credit-line preposition. It names what the thing used to be before somebody rebuilt it.
examples: A miniseries adapted from a novel nobody finished.
The recipe is adapted from my grandmother's, with half the butter.
Adapted from a 1954 radio play, the film keeps the original ending.
Figure 3 is adapted from Kessler (2011) and used with permission.
The drills are adapted from the Army's field manual.
A screenplay adapted from her own memoir — adapted by would name the writer instead.
entries.русский: по мотивам, в переработке — указывает, чем вещь была до переделки
entries.register: neutral; credit lines, playbills, textbook figures, and recipe headnotes
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a source work or its author — never a finite clause, and a gerund is impossible (✗ adapted from writing a novel).
entries.pattern: [work] adapted from [source] · Adapted from [source], [main clause].
entries.contrast: Adapted from claims a change of form — novel to screenplay, restaurant recipe to home kitchen, adult text to children's edition — and promises that the original is being followed. Based on claims only a source of material and is much looser: a film based on a true story may invent freely. In a credit line by names the adapter, not the source, so swapping the two reverses the credit; ✗ adapted of is not English, and the literary version is after (a comedy after Molière).
entries.see also: based on, as cited in, premised on, after the manner of, from

entries.meaning: The secondhand-source marker of academic writing, and the one citation formula that is honest about what the writer did not read.
examples: Vygotsky (1934), as cited in Wertsch (1985), draws the same distinction.
The 1908 figures, as cited in the commission's report, are unreliable.
He quotes Adams, as cited in a footnote to Miller's biography.
As cited in the brief, the statute has never been amended.
Reviewers flagged three claims as resting on work known only as cited in secondary sources.
The epigraph is Pascal, as cited in a sermon of 1890.
entries.русский: цит. по — научн. ссылка на источник, прочитанный из вторых рук
entries.register: formal and scholarly; APA-style citation of a source the writer reached secondhand. An American meets it in a term paper, a literature review, and a brief quoting a case from another brief.
entries.type: marginal/participial (three-word: as plus past participle plus preposition)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the work actually consulted — never a finite clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: ([author], [year], as cited in [author], [year]) · [quotation], as cited in [source]
entries.contrast: The point of the phrase is an admission: the writer read the second source, not the first. (Vygotsky, 1934, as cited in Wertsch, 1985) credits Vygotsky with the idea and Wertsch with the writer's access to it, and dropping the phrase claims a reading that never happened. Quoted in is the plainer version and the one Chicago style prefers; bare cited in points the other way, naming where a work is cited rather than where you found it. The sister phrases as defined in, as provided in, as set forth in, and as used in point into a document instead of at a source, and belong with the topic and reference prepositions.
entries.see also: as determined by, as evidenced by, as measured by, according to, per

entries.meaning: The decision-rights clause. Read it before the number it modifies.
examples: Fair market value, as determined by an independent appraiser, controls.
Benefits are payable on total disability, as determined by the plan administrator.
The bonus pool, as determined by the compensation committee, is discretionary.
Eligibility turns on household income as determined by the prior year's return.
Grades are final as determined by the instructor of record.
The boundary follows the thread of the river as determined by the 1953 survey.
entries.русский: как определено (кем-л.), по определению — юр. называет того, кто решает
entries.register: formal and legal; contracts, benefit plans, regulations, insurance policies, and grading rubrics. An American meets it in an employment agreement and in the fine print of a health plan.
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the decider — a person, an office, a committee, or a stated method. Never a finite clause (✗ as determined by the board decides), never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], as determined by [decider] · [quantity] as determined by [method]
entries.contrast: This is the clause that names who gets to decide, and in a contract it is often worth more than the sentence it modifies: fair market value as determined by an independent appraiser takes the decision away from both parties, while as determined by the Company in its sole discretion hands it to one of them. Against as measured by, which names a yardstick, and as evidenced by, which names a proof, this one names an authority. Bare by would name an agent without the parenthetical framing, and according to reports a source rather than conferring a power.
entries.see also: as measured by, as evidenced by, at the behest of, subject to, pursuant to

entries.meaning: The proof clause. It hands the reader the exhibit without breaking the sentence.
examples: The loan was repaid in full, as evidenced by the canceled note.
She had actual notice, as evidenced by her reply of March 3.
Demand is recovering, as evidenced by three straight months of hiring.
The patient is fluid-overloaded, as evidenced by an eight-pound weight gain.
The town was prosperous, as evidenced by the size of the courthouse.
He knew the risk, as evidenced by having bought insurance the week before.
entries.русский: о чём свидетельствует, что подтверждается — вводит доказательство внутри фразы
entries.register: formal; legal drafting, academic argument, and medical charting. An American meets it in a demand letter, a peer-reviewed paper, and a nurse's note.
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the proof — a document, a fact, a finding. A gerund is possible (as evidenced by having bought insurance the week before), but a nominalization reads better. Never a finite clause: ✗ as evidenced by he never called → as evidenced by his silence.
entries.pattern: [claim], as evidenced by [proof].
entries.contrast: It asserts that the thing named proves the claim just made, which is stronger than as shown by and much stronger than as indicated by, and it is why lawyers use it to bolt a claim onto an exhibit (as evidenced by the attached invoice). Against as determined by, which names who decides, this names what proves. Against judging by, which admits the speaker is inferring and might be wrong, as evidenced by admits nothing. The verb is spelled with a c: evidenced, never ✗ evidented.
entries.see also: as determined by, as cited in, judging by, based on, on the strength of

entries.meaning: The yardstick clause. Every serious number in a report should carry one.
examples: Inflation, as measured by the consumer price index, ran at three percent.
Reading gains, as measured by the state test, were largest in third grade.
The country is the world's largest economy as measured by purchasing power.
Sleep quality, as measured by the Pittsburgh index, improved in both groups.
Productivity as measured by output per hour has barely moved in a decade.
Success here is as measured by retention at twelve months, not by sales.
entries.русский: по измерению, согласно замеру — называет мерило, которым получена цифра
entries.register: formal; science, statistics, economics, policy writing, and performance reviews
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an instrument, a test, an index, or a metric — never a finite clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [claim or quantity], as measured by [metric].
entries.contrast: This is the honest hedge of quantitative writing: it concedes that the claim is only as good as the yardstick. Poverty, as measured by the federal threshold is a narrower claim than poverty, and a reader is entitled to the difference. Against as determined by, where an authority decides, and as evidenced by, where a fact proves, this one names the ruler. Controlling for is its neighbor in the same methods paragraph and does the opposite job — one names the measure, the other removes a confound — and adjusting for reworks the number itself.
entries.see also: as determined by, as evidenced by, controlling for, adjusting for, in terms of

entries.meaning: The most contested word in this file, and the clearest case of a participle finishing its journey into a preposition. When it modifies a noun (a film based on a novel) nobody objects; the argument is only about the fronted adverbial.
examples: The film is based on a novel nobody read.
They built a whole product line based on one patent.
Based on the polling, the race is a toss-up.
Based on what she told me, I'd take the offer.
We rejected the bid based on price alone.
Based on three quarters of data, the trend looks real.
Based on having watched two seasons, I'd say it holds up.

senses.head: Deriving from a source
body: Attached to a noun, uncontroversially participial.

senses.head: On the evidence of; according to
body: The fronted preposition.
examples: The film is based on a novel nobody read.
They built a whole product line based on one patent.
Based on the polling, the race is a toss-up.
Based on what she told me, I'd take the offer.
We rejected the bid based on price alone.
Based on three quarters of data, the trend looks real.
Based on having watched two seasons, I'd say it holds up.

entries.русский: на основе, по мотивам (о фильме); исходя из — судя по имеющимся данным
entries.register: neutral; standard in American journalism and business writing
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a wh-nominal (based on what he told us) — never a finite that-clause (✗ based on that he told us). For a clause, write because or on the ground that.
entries.pattern: Based on [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [noun phrase] based on [noun phrase]. · [clause], based on [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The famous dangling-modifier fight. Traditionalists object to the sentence-opening use (Based on the data, we canceled the launch) because we are not based on anything, and prescribe on the basis of or judging by instead. American practice has moved: fronted based on is now standard in edited prose. The real participle basing still needs its subject and still dangles (✗ Basing the estimate on last year, the budget was wrong). Against depending on: based on names the evidence behind a settled conclusion, depending on names the variable that has not resolved yet.
entries.see also: judging by, depending on, considering, given, according to, on the basis of

entries.meaning: The manifest word. It states where a vessel, a train, a shipment, or a life is pointed.
examples: A freighter bound for Rotterdam left the harbor at dawn.
The 6:40 is bound for Philadelphia, calling at Trenton.
Two truckloads of grain bound for the coast were turned back at the line.
He was nineteen, broke, and bound for California.
Half that graduating class was bound for medical school.
The ship was homeward bound, and the crew was bound for two weeks of leave.
entries.русский: следующий в, направляющийся в — о судне, поезде, грузе; книжн. и морской оттенок
entries.register: neutral, faintly literary and nautical; standard on manifests, in shipping news, and in headlines
entries.type: marginal (past-participial in shape, adjectival in origin, two-word)
entries.complement: a destination — a place, a port, a market, or a metaphorical end point. Never a finite clause, never a gerund, and never a person.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] bound for [destination] · [subject] is bound for [destination] · compounds: homeward bound, outward bound, northbound, Chicago-bound
entries.contrast: The bound here is not the past participle of bind: it is Old Norse búinn, "prepared," which is why bound for Chicago has nothing to do with being tied, while bound by the contract and bound to happen do come from bind. Against headed for, the ordinary spoken word, bound for is older and more formal and belongs to ships, trains, and fate; against destined for, which claims the arrival is settled, bound for reports only the heading. En route to says the journey is already under way.
entries.see also: headed for, destined for, en route to, toward, for

entries.meaning: Sets one thing beside another so the difference registers. It is the standard American way to frame a number as good or bad news.
examples: Compared to last year, sales are up nine percent.
The rent is cheap compared to Boston.
Compared to the original, the remake is tame.
Enrollment fell four percent, compared with six percent nationally.
Two hours is nothing compared to what that drive used to be.
Compared to being on call every night, this job is a vacation.

senses.head: Measured against
body: The quantitative use, the common one.

senses.head: Likened to
body: The figurative use, where the two things are of different kinds.
examples: Compared to last year, sales are up nine percent.
The rent is cheap compared to Boston.
Compared to the original, the remake is tame.
Enrollment fell four percent, compared with six percent nationally.
Two hours is nothing compared to what that drive used to be.
Compared to being on call every night, this job is a vacation.

entries.русский: по сравнению с; также «подобно, наравне с» при образном сопоставлении
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause (✗ compared to he ran faster → compared to him, compared to his time). The two things compared must be parallel, and this is where the sentence usually breaks: ✗ Her salary is low compared to a manager compares a salary to a person → compared to a manager's or compared with that of a manager. A pronoun object takes the objective case: compared to me, ✗ compared to I.
entries.pattern: [clause], compared to [noun phrase]. · Compared to [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [noun phrase] compared with [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The old rule assigned compare to to likening unlike things (shall I compare thee to a summer's day) and compare with to measuring like against like (compare this quarter with last). In the fixed participial preposition the distinction has collapsed in American English, and compared to now covers both; compared with survives as the slightly more formal and more statistical of the two. In comparison with is the heavy version, relative to the technical one. Than is a conjunction and is not an alternative here: ✗ cheaper compared than, either cheaper than or cheap compared to. And versus merely juxtaposes two things, where compared to asserts that a measurement has been made.
entries.variants: compared with (more formal, more common in statistical writing)
entries.see also: based on, given, in comparison with, relative to, contrary to

entries.meaning: The word that says where a thing will end up, not merely where it is going.
examples: Three pallets destined for the Denver warehouse never left the dock.
Most of the crop is destined for export.
The letter was destined for an archive nobody would open for fifty years.
She was, everyone agreed, destined for the bench.
The company looked destined for bankruptcy until the refinancing came through.
He was destined to lose that seat — destined for defeat says it with a noun instead.

senses.head: Consigned to a place
body: The shipping use, literal and unremarkable.

senses.head: Fated for an outcome
body: The biographical use, where the word does its heavy breathing.
examples: Three pallets destined for the Denver warehouse never left the dock.
Most of the crop is destined for export.
The letter was destined for an archive nobody would open for fifty years.
She was, everyone agreed, destined for the bench.
The company looked destined for bankruptcy until the refinancing came through.
He was destined to lose that seat — destined for defeat says it with a noun instead.

entries.русский: предназначенный для (о грузе); которому суждено (о судьбе)
entries.register: neutral to formal; logistics and shipping at one end, biography and obituary at the other
entries.complement: a destination or an outcome — a place, a market, a rank, a fate. Never a finite clause. A to-infinitive belongs to the adjective rather than to this preposition, and the two are not interchangeable: destined to fail and destined for failure are both standard, but ✗ destined for fail and ✗ destined to failure are not.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] destined for [destination] · [subject] is destined for [outcome] · [subject] is destined to [verb]
entries.contrast: Against bound for, which reports a heading, destined for claims the arrival is settled — by a shipping order, a plan, or fate — and it keeps that grandeur even on a bill of lading. Against headed for, which is neutral and spoken, it is a prediction, and predictions are what make it a cliché in profiles (destined for greatness). In logistics it is flat and literal and nobody hears the fate in it at all.
entries.see also: bound for, headed for, en route to, for, toward

entries.meaning: The running-order preposition. It sets two things in sequence and refuses to say that the first caused the second.
examples: Rain in the morning, followed by clearing in the afternoon.
The ceremony is at four, followed by a reception in the courtyard.
Sear the meat, followed by the onions and garlic.
A short speech followed by questions from the floor.
Two quarters of losses, followed by the sharpest rebound in a decade.
Each witness reads the statement aloud, followed by signing every page.
entries.русский: за которым следует, а затем — порядок следования без утверждения о причине
entries.register: neutral; programs, itineraries, recipes, forecasts, and lab methods
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (followed by signing every page) — never a finite clause (✗ followed by they left).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], followed by [noun phrase] · [main clause], followed by [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The converse of preceded by, and the passive counterpart of the preposition following: A followed by B and B following A put the same two events in the same order, and mixing the two forms reverses the sequence. The reliable test is that whatever comes after followed by happens second. Unlike following, it makes no causal claim at all, which is why forecasts and programs prefer it. Being a reduced passive, it attaches to the nearest noun and can misfire: We had dinner followed by a walk is fine, but We heard from the mayor followed by the fire chief invites a reading in which the mayor is being chased.
entries.see also: preceded by, following, preceding, after, prior to

entries.meaning: Treats what follows as established and reasons from it. Its origin is visible in the mathematical use, where the given is literally what you are handed at the start of a proof.
examples: Given the circumstances, the sentence was lenient.
Given his record, the promotion surprised nobody.
Given the shortage of nurses, the wait is no surprise.
Given that she had two days to prepare, the presentation was remarkable.
Given that no one objected, the motion carried.
Given two points, construct the perpendicular bisector.
Given a constant rate of decay, the age can be calculated.
At any given moment, half the fleet is in the shop — and that the schedule slips is now a given.

senses.head: In view of; taking as established
body: The everyday use, with a noun phrase.

senses.head: Given that (with a clause)
body: The same meaning, with a full finite clause — one of only three words in this file that allows one in ordinary prose, alongside considering and granted; the fourth, legal notwithstanding that, is confined to drafting.

senses.head: In mathematics and logic: assumed as a starting condition
Cross-class: the adjective and the noun
body: A given moment, a given. No object, no clause — and no longer a preposition.
examples: Given the circumstances, the sentence was lenient.
Given his record, the promotion surprised nobody.
Given the shortage of nurses, the wait is no surprise.
Given that she had two days to prepare, the presentation was remarkable.
Given that no one objected, the motion carried.
Given two points, construct the perpendicular bisector.
Given a constant rate of decay, the age can be calculated.
At any given moment, half the fleet is in the shop — and that the schedule slips is now a given.

entries.русский: учитывая, ввиду; given that — «раз уж, поскольку»; в математике — «дано»
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a finite clause with that — given that the deadline had passed. It cannot stand alone as an adverb (✗ She did well, given).
entries.pattern: Given [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Given that [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] given [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: Against considering: given states a premise and moves on, while considering weighs and often excuses. Against granted: given takes a fact you both accept; granted concedes a point you are about to argue past. Only considering and granted can trail a sentence with no complement at all; given always needs an object. Cross-class, three other words are spelled the same and none of them is this preposition: the plain past participle of give (the money was given anonymously), the attributive adjective meaning "specified" or "prone to" (at any given moment, given to exaggeration), and the count noun (that's a given). The preposition is the one that takes a bare object and modifies the whole clause.
entries.see also: granted, considering, based on, notwithstanding, in view of

entries.meaning: The concessive of the pair. It hands the other side a point and then takes the sentence back.
examples: Granted the difficulty of the terrain, the survey was fast work.
Granted that the data are thin, the pattern is still suggestive.
Granted, the seats are terrible, but the sound is perfect.
It's a risk, granted, and we're taking it anyway.
Granting his sincerity, the argument still fails.
Granted the premise, the conclusion follows.

senses.head: Conceding a stated point (with an object or clause)
Standing alone as admittedly
body: No complement, comma after.
examples: Granted the difficulty of the terrain, the survey was fast work.
Granted that the data are thin, the pattern is still suggestive.
Granted, the seats are terrible, but the sound is perfect.
It's a risk, granted, and we're taking it anyway.
Granting his sincerity, the argument still fails.
Granted the premise, the conclusion follows.

entries.русский: допустим, положим, спору нет — уступка собеседнику перед возражением
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: marginal/participial (past participle); also a standalone concessive adverb
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a finite clause with or without that — granted (that) the price is high. It also takes no complement at all as a sentence adverb: Granted, it's expensive.
entries.pattern: Granted [noun phrase], [main clause]. · Granted (that) [clause], [main clause]. · Granted, [main clause].
entries.contrast: Given accepts a premise as neutral fact; granted concedes a point that works against the speaker, and the sentence that follows almost always pushes back — Granted, it's expensive, but.... As a bare adverb it takes a comma and functions like admittedly; given can never do this. The -ing variant granting (that) is slightly more formal and less common.
entries.see also: given, considering, notwithstanding, in spite of

entries.meaning: The direction-of-travel word of American speech, for cars, careers, and marriages alike.
examples: Where are you headed to after this?
They're headed for the airport now.
The bill looked headed for a veto until the last week of the session.
That marriage was headed for trouble from the first year.
We were headed to Nashville and got as far as Memphis.
Both teams are headed for the playoffs for the first time since 1998.

senses.head: Traveling toward a place
body: With to or for.

senses.head: On course for an outcome
body: With for only.
examples: Where are you headed to after this?
They're headed for the airport now.
The bill looked headed for a veto until the last week of the session.
That marriage was headed for trouble from the first year.
We were headed to Nashville and got as far as Memphis.
Both teams are headed for the playoffs for the first time since 1998.

entries.русский: направляющийся в, идущий к — разг. о машине, карьере, браке
entries.register: informal to neutral; the everyday spoken American form
entries.complement: a destination or an outcome — a place, a state of affairs. Never a finite clause, never a gerund (✗ headed for leaving).
entries.pattern: [subject] is headed for [destination] · [subject] is headed to [place] · Where are you headed?
entries.contrast: American English says headed for and headed to where British English says heading for; both American forms are standard, and the split between them is reach — headed to wants a place, while headed for also takes an abstract outcome (headed for a fall, headed for divorce, where ✗ headed to trouble sounds wrong). Against bound for, which is formal and belongs to ships and trains, and destined for, which predicts the ending, headed for reports only the current direction and leaves the ending open.
entries.variants: headed to, heading for, heading to (all current; heading for is the British default)
entries.see also: bound for, destined for, en route to, toward, back to

entries.meaning: The escalator clause in one word. It says a number will follow another number wherever it goes.
examples: Social Security payments are indexed to the consumer price index.
The lease sets a base rent indexed to inflation.
Pensions indexed to wage growth cost the state more every year.
Executive pay was indexed to three-year total shareholder return.
Support obligations indexed to the payer's income are recalculated each January.
A bond indexed to the price of oil pays more when crude does.
entries.русский: индексируемый по, привязанный к — сумма автоматически следует за другим показателем
entries.register: formal; economics, benefits administration, tax law, and contract drafting. An American meets it every year in the Social Security cost-of-living notice.
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an index or benchmark — never a finite clause, never a gerund, never a person. In running speech the two /t/ sounds collapse into one: indexed to comes out /ˈɪndɛkstə/.
entries.pattern: [payment or figure] indexed to [benchmark]
entries.contrast: Pegged to fixes a value at a defended ratio and belongs to currencies; indexed to makes a figure move with a published measure and belongs to wages, benefits, rents, and tax brackets. Tied to is the plain word for both. Against adjusting for, which reworks a number after the fact, indexing builds the adjustment into the future so nobody has to argue about it again.
entries.see also: pegged to, referenced to, adjusting for, in proportion to, relative to

entries.meaning: The fixed-exchange word, borrowed by editors for the reason a story runs today rather than next month.
examples: The riyal has been pegged to the dollar since 1986.
Fees are pegged to the prime rate and change when it does.
Salaries pegged to the federal scale rose two percent.
The magazine ran a package pegged to the fiftieth anniversary.
Ticket prices are pegged to what the market bore last season.
A currency pegged to a basket of three others is harder to attack.

senses.head: Fixed to a benchmark
body: The financial sense.

senses.head: Tied to an occasion
body: The journalistic sense.
examples: The riyal has been pegged to the dollar since 1986.
Fees are pegged to the prime rate and change when it does.
Salaries pegged to the federal scale rose two percent.
The magazine ran a package pegged to the fiftieth anniversary.
Ticket prices are pegged to what the market bore last season.
A currency pegged to a basket of three others is harder to attack.

entries.русский: привязанный к — о курсе валюты; в журналистике — приуроченный к событию
entries.register: neutral to formal; financial journalism, central banking, and newsroom shop talk
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a benchmark — a currency, a rate, an index — or, in the journalistic sense, an occasion. Never a finite clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [currency or figure] pegged to [benchmark] · [story] pegged to [occasion]
entries.contrast: A peg is fixed and defended: the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. dollar inside a band, and breaking the peg is front-page news. Indexed to is a formula that moves; pegged to is a promise to hold still. The newsroom sense comes from the noun news peg, the occasion that justifies running a story now, and it is idiomatic American shop talk rather than finance. Note the doubled g before the ending.
entries.see also: indexed to, referenced to, based on, relative to, in proportion to

entries.meaning: The earlier-event preposition. It backs a sentence up one step without starting a new one.
examples: The vote was preceded by four hours of debate.
Each rehearsal is preceded by a half hour of warm-ups.
The eruption was preceded by weeks of small tremors.
A short blackout, preceded by a flicker, took out the whole block.
The interview, preceded by a tour of the plant, ran two hours long.
Every visit is preceded by signing the visitors' book.
entries.русский: которому предшествует — отступает на шаг назад во времени, не начиная новой фразы
entries.register: neutral to formal; description, procedure, scholarship, and captions
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (preceded by signing the visitors' book) — never a finite clause (✗ preceded by she spoke).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], preceded by [noun phrase] · [main clause], preceded by [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The converse of followed by, and together they are the most reliable way to fix an order in writing without dates: whatever comes after preceded by happened first. Reversing them reverses the history, and the error is common in captions and in lab methods. Preceded by is the passive counterpart of the preposition preceding and, like it, asserts nothing about cause — for that you need following or in the wake of.
entries.see also: followed by, preceding, following, before, prior to

entries.meaning: The load-bearing-assumption word. It names the thing that, if it goes, takes everything else with it.
examples: The whole plan is predicated on the state approving the permit.
Federal jurisdiction here is predicated on diversity of citizenship.
Their offer was predicated on a clean environmental report.
The forecast is predicated on rates falling by summer — ✗ predicated on rates will fall.
Everything we agreed to was predicated on being able to refinance.
The argument is predicated upon a distinction the statute does not draw.
entries.русский: основанный на, исходящий из — книжн./юр. о посылке, без которой рушится всё остальное
entries.register: formal; law, policy, and academic argument. Outside those settings it reads as inflation, and based on is the better word.
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (predicated on being able to refinance) — never a finite clause (✗ predicated on rates would fall → predicated on rates falling, or on the assumption that rates would fall). The on is a preposition, so a verb after it takes -ing: ✗ predicated on refinance, ✗ predicated to refinance.
entries.pattern: [claim or plan] is predicated on [noun phrase or gerund]
entries.contrast: Based on is the plain word and is nearly always better. Predicated on makes a stronger claim: the thing would collapse without the premise, so a plan predicated on one assumption fails the moment the assumption does. Premised on is its twin and is now the commoner of the two in American legal writing. Keep it apart from the logician's predicate of, which asserts a property of a subject and takes a different preposition entirely.
entries.see also: premised on, based on, given, subject to, on the basis of

entries.meaning: The assumption word of the brief-writer. It marks the plank that the rest of the argument is standing on.
examples: The suit is premised on a theory the Ninth Circuit rejected last year.
Their whole strategy was premised on cheap money.
The estimate is premised on the market recovering by fall.
An apology premised on being misunderstood is not an apology.
The rule is premised upon the idea that notice is always possible.
The deal was premised on a regulatory approval that never came.
entries.русский: построенный на допущении, исходящий из посылки — книжн., язык юр. записок
entries.register: formal; American legal briefs and academic prose
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (premised on the market recovering) — never a finite clause (✗ premised on the market recovers). For a clause, switch the frame entirely and write on the premise that the market will recover. Also ✗ premised to, ✗ premised in.
entries.pattern: [claim] is premised on [noun phrase or gerund] · on the premise that [clause] — the clause repair
entries.contrast: Against predicated on, the two are interchangeable in nearly every sentence, and American courts write premised on more often. Against based on, which names the evidence behind a conclusion, premised on names the assumption the argument cannot do without. The word is stressed on the first syllable, like the noun premise, and it is historically the same word as premises meaning a building — the things "set before" in a deed — which is a piece of etymology worth knowing precisely so the two do not get mixed in a sentence.
entries.see also: predicated on, based on, given, on the grounds of, subject to

entries.meaning: The datum word. It names the zero, without which every other number on the page is an opinion.
examples: All voltages in the diagram are referenced to chassis ground.
Elevations are referenced to the North American Vertical Datum of 1988.
Power expressed in dBm is referenced to one milliwatt.
Each reading is referenced to a calibrated standard kept in the lab.
Coordinates referenced to the wrong datum put the well a hundred feet off.
Timing is referenced to the rising edge of the clock.
entries.русский: отсчитываемый от, относительно (нуля) — тех. называет точку отсчёта измерения
entries.register: technical; electrical engineering, metrology, surveying, and lab science. Outside those fields it reads as jargon.
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a reference point, datum, or baseline — never a finite clause, never a gerund, never a person.
entries.pattern: [measurement] referenced to [datum]
entries.contrast: In technical writing referenced to names the zero a measurement was taken from, and the number means nothing without it: a voltage referenced to ground, an elevation referenced to mean sea level, a power level referenced to one milliwatt — which is all that the dBm scale is. Relative to is the general-purpose word and the better one in nontechnical prose; indexed to and pegged to do the same job for money. Keep it away from the loose journalistic verb referenced, meaning "mentioned" (he referenced the memo), which many American editors still refuse.
entries.see also: indexed to, pegged to, as measured by, relative to, to

entries.meaning: Joins two names for one person and says nothing about which came first.
examples: The indictment names Robert Ellis, alias Bobby Deal.
Edward Teach, alias Blackbeard, blockaded the harbor for a week.
The witness knew him only as Sam Price, a.k.a. Samuel Prizzi.
She writes crime novels as J. R. Vance, a.k.a. Professor Vance of the English department.
Court records list the defendant as Doe, a/k/a Roe, a/k/a Coe.
They call it the Family Tax Relief Act, a.k.a. the landlord bonus.

senses.head: Introducing an assumed or additional name
body: The formal and forensic use.

senses.head: a.k.a.: the everyday form
body: Including the jocular renaming of things and institutions.
examples: The indictment names Robert Ellis, alias Bobby Deal.
Edward Teach, alias Blackbeard, blockaded the harbor for a week.
The witness knew him only as Sam Price, a.k.a. Samuel Prizzi.
She writes crime novels as J. R. Vance, a.k.a. Professor Vance of the English department.
Court records list the defendant as Doe, a/k/a Roe, a/k/a Coe.
They call it the Family Tax Relief Act, a.k.a. the landlord bonus.

entries.русский: он же, известный также как — соединяет два имени одного человека, не уточняя порядок
entries.register: formal in a court caption, otherwise flavored by crime fiction; the abbreviation a.k.a. is the ordinary American form and is at home in conversation
entries.type: marginal (a Latin adverb, "at another time," pressed into prepositional service)
entries.complement: a name, and nothing else — never a clause, never a gerund, and never a common noun (✗ alias a plumber). It takes no article and no comma of its own on the right: Robert Ellis, alias Bobby Deal.
entries.pattern: [name] alias [name] · [name] a.k.a. [name] · [name] a/k/a [name] (the court-caption spelling)
entries.contrast: Four naming words divide the work. Alias introduces a second name for the same person; née introduces the name a woman was born with; d/b/a introduces the trade name of a business; and qua introduces a capacity rather than a name at all. In American court captions a/k/a has almost entirely replaced alias, which now sounds like a paperback; a.k.a. is also the only member of the group used jokingly (the tax bill, a.k.a. the landlord bonus), and it is read out letter by letter. Keep the preposition apart from the count noun an alias, which takes an article and is not this word.
entries.variants: a.k.a., aka, a/k/a (all read "ay-kay-ay"); the archaic full form is Latin alias dictus
entries.see also: née, d/b/a, qua, in the person of, in the capacity of

entries.ipa: /ˌdi bi ˈeɪ/, in full /ˈduɪŋ ˈbɪznəs æz/
entries.meaning: The business-identity connector. It is how a filing says that the sign on the door and the name on the lawsuit belong to the same entity.
examples: The caption reads Ellis Holdings LLC d/b/a Sunrise Diner.
She sued the contractor, Delgado d/b/a Del's Roofing.
Payments went to a checking account for Vance Media d/b/a The Weekly.
The plaintiff, Meridian Health Systems f/k/a Meridian Hospital Corp., filed in March.
Title now stands in the name of Kestrel Partners n/k/a Kestrel Capital LLC.
Register the d/b/a with the county before you order the checks.

senses.head: Naming the trade name of a business
body: The d/b/a use proper.

senses.head: Tracking a change of name
body: F/k/a and n/k/a, in captions and title records.
examples: The caption reads Ellis Holdings LLC d/b/a Sunrise Diner.
She sued the contractor, Delgado d/b/a Del's Roofing.
Payments went to a checking account for Vance Media d/b/a The Weekly.
The plaintiff, Meridian Health Systems f/k/a Meridian Hospital Corp., filed in March.
Title now stands in the name of Kestrel Partners n/k/a Kestrel Capital LLC.
Register the d/b/a with the county before you order the checks.

entries.русский: юр. действующий под фирменным наименованием — связывает лицо и вывеску на двери
entries.register: legal and commercial; court captions, county filings, business licenses, invoices, and bank signature cards
entries.type: marginal (an abbreviated participial phrase, doing business as, used as a preposition)
entries.complement: a trade name — never a clause, never a gerund. The order is fixed and legally load-bearing: the legal name comes first and the trade name second, and reversing them misstates who can be sued.
entries.pattern: [legal name] d/b/a [trade name] · [former name] f/k/a [current name] · [old name] n/k/a [new name]
entries.contrast: D/b/a links a legal person to the name it trades under — in Ellis Holdings LLC d/b/a Sunrise Diner, the LLC is the party and the diner is only the sign. F/k/a ("formerly known as") and n/k/a ("now known as") track a change of name over time, and they point in opposite directions: f/k/a looks back from the name in use now, n/k/a looks forward from the old one, so picking the wrong one puts the timeline backwards. A.k.a. covers any second name at all. The British equivalent of d/b/a is trading as, abbreviated t/a.
entries.variants: dba, DBA, d.b.a.; the same frame gives f/k/a, n/k/a, and a/k/a
entries.see also: alias, née, qua, in the name of, in the capacity of

entries.meaning: Records the name somebody was born with, in the one construction English kept from French for the purpose.
examples: Survived by his wife, Margaret Ellis, née Doyle.
The bride's mother, Anne Whitcomb, née Fairbanks, gave the toast.
Bob Dylan, né Robert Zimmerman, was twenty when he got to New York.
The parish register lists Sarah Pool, née Hutchins, of Salem.
My grandmother, née Kowalczyk, shortened it to Coles at Ellis Island.
The Willis Tower, né the Sears Tower, is still called by the old name.
entries.pronunciation note: NAY, rhyming with day and never NEE
entries.русский: урождённая — девичья фамилия женщины
entries.register: formal; obituaries, wedding announcements, genealogies, and society pages, with a growing jocular use in journalism
entries.type: marginal (a French past participle, "born," used as a preposition)
entries.complement: a name — in the strict use, the family name alone. Never a clause, never a gerund. Because née already means "born," the given name is not repeated: Hillary Clinton, née Rodham, and ✗ née Hillary Rodham is common but frowned on.
entries.pattern: [married name], née [birth surname] · [current name], né [former name of a man]
entries.contrast: Née is feminine and né masculine, and using née of a man is the error that turns up most (Bob Dylan, né Robert Zimmerman). Against alias, which names an assumed identity, née records a fact of birth and passes no judgment; against plain formerly, which says nothing about why the name changed. American writing accepts the unaccented spelling nee, and American obituaries often prefer a parenthesis or the word born instead. The playful extension to renamed things (the Willis Tower, né the Sears Tower) is journalism, not standard usage.
entries.see also: alias, d/b/a, qua, in the person of

entries.meaning: Marks the person who did not know, and hands the reader the information first.
examples: Unbeknownst to her parents, she had already signed the lease.
The camera had been running for an hour, unbeknownst to everyone in the room.
Unbeknownst to the board, two directors had already resigned.
He kept a second policy, unbeknownst to his wife.
Unbeknownst to the buyers, the roof had been patched three times.
The two firms were bidding against each other, unbeknownst to either of them.
entries.русский: без ведома (кого-л.), незаметно для — читатель уже знает, а персонаж ещё нет
entries.register: neutral to formal, with a storytelling flavor; common in narrative journalism and fiction, rare in technical writing
entries.type: marginal (a fossilized adjective that takes a bare object, two-word)
entries.complement: a person or an institution — the party kept in the dark. Never a finite clause (✗ unbeknownst to he was there), never a gerund, and not an inanimate force (✗ unbeknownst to the weather).
entries.pattern: Unbeknownst to [person], [main clause]. · [main clause], unbeknownst to [person].
entries.contrast: The -st is a late and illogical addition — unbeknown is the older form, beknown has been dead for centuries, and there is no ✗ beknownst to — so the word survives only inside this frame. American usage prefers unbeknownst, British unbeknown, and both are standard. Against without X knowing, which is the plain equivalent and often better; against behind X's back, which adds a charge of bad faith that unbeknownst to does not carry. It has a narrative habit worth noticing: it almost always sets up a reveal.
entries.see also: absent, without, in the absence of, behind, worth

entries.meaning: The reason worth sits in this file is that it is the one common English word that takes a direct object without being a verb or a preposition by traditional labeling. Every modern grammar that reclassifies it makes it a preposition.
examples: The house is worth about four hundred thousand.
That coin is worth more than the car it came in.
The drive is long, but the view is worth it.
This place is worth visiting twice.
It's worth asking before you assume.
The old boiler is not worth repairing a third time.
For what it's worth, I'd have made the same call.
The agent played up the school district for all it was worth.
We got twenty dollars' worth of gas and our money's worth of advice.

senses.head: Deserving the time, money, or trouble
body: Typically with a gerund — and the gerund is where learners reach for the infinitive and go wrong.

senses.head: In fixed phrases
body: For what it's worth, for all it's worth.

senses.head: Cross-class: the noun
body: Preceded by a possessive and followed by of, which the preposition never is: a dollar's worth of trouble.
examples: The house is worth about four hundred thousand.
That coin is worth more than the car it came in.
The drive is long, but the view is worth it.
This place is worth visiting twice.
It's worth asking before you assume.
The old boiler is not worth repairing a third time.
For what it's worth, I'd have made the same call.
The agent played up the school district for all it was worth.
We got twenty dollars' worth of gas and our money's worth of advice.

entries.pronunciation note: run together before a weak object: worth it /ˈwɜrθ ɪt/ → /ˈwɜrθət/ — WURTH
entries.русский: стоимостью в; стоящий того, чтобы — worth seeing «стоит посмотреть» (только с герундием)
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: marginal (traditionally labeled an adjective, but it takes a bare object like a preposition)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause and never a to-infinitive: ✗ worth to see, ✗ worth to be seen → worth seeing. This is one of the most common learner errors in English. The object may be a pronoun: worth it.
entries.pattern: [subject] is worth [noun phrase] · [subject] is worth [verb-ing] · it is worth [verb-ing] · for what it's worth
entries.contrast: Worth takes its object bare; worthy requires of — worth praise but worthy of praise; ✗ worth of praise is the error that comes of mixing them. And the gerund after worth is passive in meaning even though it is active in form: the house is worth fixing up means worth being fixed up, and adding being is wrong (✗ worth being fixed up). Keep the preposition apart from the identical noun, which follows a possessive and takes of: ten dollars' worth of gas, get your money's worth. Note the apostrophe — the measure is possessive, and ten dollars worth is a misspelling.
entries.see also: going on, absent, come, effective

entries.meaning: Descended from the past participle of Old English āgān, "to pass by," so it is a participial preposition too — one that finished its journey centuries earlier than the rest of this file and ended up on the wrong side of its object.
examples: Three weeks ago we had no idea.
She called a few minutes ago.
That happened long ago.
The factory closed twenty years ago.
I saw him not five minutes ago.
A century ago, none of this existed.
entries.русский: тому назад — стоит после меры времени: three weeks ago «три недели назад»
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: precedes it — a measure-of-time noun phrase (three weeks, a moment, long). It can take nothing after it, ever, and never a clause. The measure phrase is obligatory: ✗ He left ago.
entries.pattern: [measure of time] ago · ✗ ago [measure of time]
entries.contrast: Two rules. First, ago counts back from now and therefore demands the simple past: ✗ He has left three days ago → He left three days ago. Before counts back from a point already in the past: He had left three days before. Second, ago is not interchangeable with for — ago locates an event, for measures a duration (she left three days ago, she was gone for three days). And long since is not a British substitute for long ago, as it is sometimes labeled: it is standard formal American English, and it differs by tense, taking the perfect that ago forbids (the shop has long since closed, ✗ the shop has closed long ago).
entries.see also: back, hence, going on, prior to

entries.meaning: Sets a topic to one side so the sentence can get to the real point. Almost always fronted as a clause-opening phrase with a comma.
examples: Cost apart, the plan is workable.
Joking apart, we need an answer by noon.
Politics apart, the two men were friends for forty years.
That one incident apart, the trip was flawless.
Style apart, the argument is sound.
entries.русский: если оставить в стороне — брит. оттенок; joking apart «шутки в сторону»
entries.register: neutral; slightly British in this construction
entries.complement: precedes it — a noun phrase or gerund. Never a clause.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] apart, [main clause].
entries.contrast: Aside is the American default in this frame: joking aside is idiomatic in the U.S., while joking apart reads as British. Do not confuse the postposed apart with the fronted complex preposition apart from, which means "except for" or "in addition to," is itself the British-leaning counterpart of aside from, and lives with the multi-word prepositions. Cross-class, the test is whether anything is being set aside: the postpositive has an object in front of it (cost apart), while the plain adverb has no object at all (the two men drifted apart, I can't tell them apart).
entries.see also: aside, aside from, excepted, apart from

entries.meaning: Brackets an objection or a topic and moves past it. It is the standard way to signal that you know about the thing you are not going to discuss.
examples: Money aside, the schedule alone kills the project.
Joking aside, that was dangerous.
All modesty aside, I fixed it in ten minutes.
The lighting aside, the room is perfect.
Legal questions aside, is this the right thing to do?
entries.русский: если оставить в стороне — амер. предпочтение; joking aside «шутки в сторону»
entries.register: neutral; the American preference over apart
entries.complement: precedes it — a noun phrase or gerund. Never a clause.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] aside, [main clause].
entries.contrast: Same job as postposed apart, but this is the form Americans use. Note the direction change when it moves to the front: postposed aside only sets something to one side, while fronted aside from can mean either "except for" or "in addition to." Cross-class, the postpositive has an object in front of it (money aside); the ordinary adverb has none (step aside, set it aside), and there is also the theatrical noun an aside.
entries.see also: aside from, apart, excepted, notwithstanding

entries.meaning: The most useful and most treacherous member of this group, because both of its meanings are common and neither is marked.
examples: Aside from the ending, the movie is terrific.
Aside from a sore shoulder, he came through fine.
Aside from the tuition, there are books and fees.
Aside from being late, she brought the wrong file.
Nobody knew, aside from the two of us.
Aside from Nashville, the tour hits four cities in Texas.

senses.head: Except for
body: Subtractive: it takes the named thing out of the claim.

senses.head: In addition to
body: Additive: it puts the named thing alongside what follows.
examples: Aside from the ending, the movie is terrific.
Aside from a sore shoulder, he came through fine.
Aside from the tuition, there are books and fees.
Aside from being late, she brought the wrong file.
Nobody knew, aside from the two of us.
Aside from Nashville, the tour hits four cities in Texas.

entries.русский: кроме, помимо — двузначно: и «за исключением», и «вдобавок к»; смысл решает контекст
entries.register: neutral; the American counterpart to British-leaning apart from
entries.type: complex, built on the postpositive aside
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a bare finite clause; use aside from the fact that if you must have one.
entries.pattern: Aside from [noun phrase], [main clause]. · [main clause] aside from [noun phrase].
entries.contrast: The ambiguity is the point of the entry. Aside from has two opposite readings — subtractive ("except for") and additive ("in addition to") — and only the following clause tells you which: Aside from the salary, the job is great subtracts, while Aside from the salary, there are benefits adds. When it matters, write except for for the first and besides or in addition to for the second. Apart from carries exactly the same double reading and is the British preference.
entries.see also: aside, apart, excluding, apart from, except for, in addition to

entries.meaning: The conversational alternative to ago, restricted to loose measures of past time.
examples: A few years back, this was all farmland.
I ran into him a while back.
Two summers back, the river came up over the road.
She mentioned it a couple of weeks back.
Some time back, they stopped answering the phone.
entries.русский: тому назад — разг. вариант ago о приблизительном сроке: a while back «недавно»
entries.register: informal; spoken American English
entries.complement: precedes it — a measure-of-time noun phrase (a few years, a while). Never a clause, and no object after it.
entries.pattern: [measure of time] back
entries.contrast: It is a casual ago, and it is vaguer — a few years back invites less precision than three years ago. Do not confuse it with the adverbial back in 1998, which comes before its object and is a different construction entirely. Cross-class, the postpositive needs a measure phrase in front of it (a while back), while the ordinary directional adverb needs nothing (come back, she called back), and back is also a common noun and a verb. In writing above the level of a blog post, use ago.
entries.see also: ago, hence, going on

entries.meaning: Takes someone or something out from under a rule that has just been stated.
examples: Everyone in that office is useless, present company excepted.
All fees are refundable, the application fee excepted.
Sundays excepted, the desk is staffed from eight to six.
The rule binds every member, the treasurer excepted.
Two counties excepted, the state went the other way.
entries.русский: за исключением (после дополнения) — present company excepted «присутствующие не в счёт»
entries.register: formal; one fixed phrase is conversational
entries.complement: precedes it — a noun phrase. Never a clause, never anything after it.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] excepted, [main clause]. · [main clause], [noun phrase] excepted.
entries.contrast: The postposed partner of prepositive excepting, and the negative counterpart of postposed included. Against excluded: excepted lifts a person or case out of a general statement, usually as a courtesy or a legal reservation, while excluded removes an item from a price, a set, or a policy. The fixed phrase present company excepted is the one use every American speaker knows.
entries.see also: excepting, excluded, included, saving

entries.meaning: Removes an item from a price, a set, or a scope of coverage, after the fact.
examples: The rate is $220 a night, taxes excluded.
All finishes are covered, custom colors excluded.
Delivery is free nationwide, Alaska and Hawaii excluded.
Every department gained headcount, contractors excluded.
The warranty covers parts and labor, wear items excluded.
entries.русский: не считая, без учёта (после дополнения) — коммерч./тех. изъятие из цены или охвата
entries.register: neutral; commercial and technical
entries.complement: precedes it — a noun phrase. Never a clause.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] excluded, [main clause]. · [main clause], [noun phrase] excluded.
entries.contrast: The mirror of postposed included and the postposed partner of excluding. Against excepted: excluded is arithmetic — it takes an item out of a total or a coverage list — while excepted is a concession about people or cases. On a price tag, tax excluded and excluding tax say the same thing; tax excepted does not exist.
entries.see also: excluding, included, excepted, exclusive of

entries.meaning: An archaic-flavored survivor. Almost every modern American use of temporal hence is either legal drafting or a bid for gravity.
examples: The lease expires two years hence.
A century hence, none of these arguments will matter.
The court will reconvene thirty days hence.
What we decide today will be judged a generation hence.
Six months hence, the program will be reviewed.
The bridge was out; hence the four-hour detour.
She had never been told; hence her surprise.

senses.head: Postpositive: a stated span from now
body: A measure of time comes first, and nothing follows.

senses.head: Cross-class: the connective adverb
body: Meaning "therefore," with no measure phrase and no object — not a preposition at all.
examples: The lease expires two years hence.
A century hence, none of these arguments will matter.
The court will reconvene thirty days hence.
What we decide today will be judged a generation hence.
Six months hence, the program will be reviewed.
The bridge was out; hence the four-hour detour.
She had never been told; hence her surprise.

entries.русский: спустя, через (после меры времени) — книжн. two years hence «через два года»
entries.register: formal and literary
entries.complement: precedes it — a measure-of-time noun phrase (three days, a week, a fortnight). Never a clause, nothing after it.
entries.pattern: [measure of time] hence
entries.contrast: The forward-pointing twin of ago: three days ago looks back, three days hence looks forward. In ordinary American English the phrase is three days from now; hence in this sense is a deliberate literary choice. Keep it apart from the far more common conjunctive adverb hence meaning "therefore," which is the same spelling doing an entirely different job. The test is the measure phrase: the postpositive has one in front of it (two years hence), and the connective adverb has none and instead points back at a whole clause (The road was closed; hence the detour). A third, obsolete sense is spatial and means "from here," surviving only in get thee hence and in henceforth.
entries.see also: ago, back, going on, pending

entries.meaning: Folds a member back into a set that has just been described, usually with a small note of surprise or self-implication.
examples: Everyone laughed, the judge included.
We all missed it, myself included.
The price is $1,800, shipping included.
Every account was affected, the founders' included.
Four states voted against, ours included.
entries.русский: включая (стоит после дополнения) — myself included «включая меня самого»
entries.register: neutral
entries.case matters: myself included and me included are both idiomatic; ✗ I included is not.
entries.complement: precedes it — a noun phrase. Never a clause.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] included, [main clause]. · [main clause], [noun phrase] included.
entries.contrast: The postposed partner of including, and it is often the more natural order when the object is a pronoun — everyone, myself included beats everyone, including myself. Its negatives are excluded for items and excepted for people.
entries.see also: including, excluded, excepted, counting, inclusive

entries.meaning: The belt-and-suspenders word. It exists because to does not say whether the last item is in or out, and sometimes that has to be settled on paper.
examples: Sections 4 to 9 inclusive are hereby repealed.
The offer is open December 1 to December 24 inclusive.
Answer questions 1 to 20 inclusive.
Rates apply Monday to Friday inclusive.
The survey covers the years 1990 to 2000 inclusive.
Read chapters 3 to 7 inclusive before the seminar.
entries.русский: включительно — офиц. отмечает, что последний пункт диапазона входит в него
entries.register: formal; contracts, statutes, and specifications
entries.type: postpositive (traditionally labeled an adjective, but it follows and governs the range in front of it)
entries.complement: precedes it — a stated range, normally two numbers or dates joined by to (1 to 30 inclusive). Never a clause, and nothing may follow it. When something does follow, the word is the prepositive complex preposition inclusive of, which is a different construction (a fee inclusive of tax).
entries.pattern: [start] to [end] inclusive · [range] inclusive
entries.contrast: This is the British repair for exactly the ambiguity American English fixes with through. Monday to Friday inclusive and Monday through Friday name the same five days, but the American form is shorter and is the default in the United States — so an American writes inclusive only in a contract or a specification where nothing may be left to inference. Its opposite postposes the same way: pages 40 to 62 exclusive leaves out page 62. Keep it apart from the ordinary attributive adjective, which stands in front of its noun and means something entirely different (an inclusive definition, an inclusive community); the postpositive has a range in front of it and the attributive has a noun behind it.
entries.see also: through, included, excluded, exclusive of, up to

entries.meaning: Three things qualify it for this file: the inclusive endpoint, which is a genuine grammatical resource American English has and British English does not; the postposed adverbial, a frozen relic in which the object comes first; and the clean cross-class split between the preposition and the object-less adverb.
examples: The office is open Monday through Friday.
Read pages 40 through 62 for tomorrow.
The exhibit runs June 3 through September 8.
Applications are accepted March through May.
The baby cried the whole night through.
She stayed loyal to him his life through.
The gate was jammed, so we squeezed through.
Read the contract through before you sign it.
Two hours in, I was through with the whole argument.

senses.head: Inclusive range
body: From the first named point to the second, with the second one counted in.

senses.head: Postposed: for the entire span
body: Fixed and literary — the whole night through.

senses.head: Cross-class: adverb, particle, predicate adjective
body: No object anywhere.
examples: The office is open Monday through Friday.
Read pages 40 through 62 for tomorrow.
The exhibit runs June 3 through September 8.
Applications are accepted March through May.
The baby cried the whole night through.
She stayed loyal to him his life through.
The gate was jammed, so we squeezed through.
Read the contract through before you sign it.
Two hours in, I was through with the whole argument.

entries.русский: по ... включительно — амер. Monday through Friday «с понедельника по пятницу включительно»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: simple preposition; in the inclusive-range sense a distinctly American connector; postpositive in fixed adverbials; also an adverb, a verb particle, and a predicate adjective
entries.complement: in the range sense, a second date, day, or number, with the first one preceding: Monday through Friday, pages 40 through 62. Never a clause. In the postposed adverbial, the noun phrase comes first: the whole night through. As an adverb and as a particle it takes no object at all — that absence is the test.
entries.pattern: [start] through [end] · [noun phrase] through (postposed adverbial) · [verb] through (adverb or particle, no object) · be through with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: This is the most useful Americanism in the whole file. American Monday through Friday includes Friday. Monday to Friday is ambiguous and British-leaning, and until Friday or till Friday excludes it — I'm here until Friday means you leave on Friday, I'm here through Friday means you leave after it. British writers reach for Monday to Friday inclusive to get the same certainty an American gets from through. Cross-class, the test is the object: the preposition has one (we drove through the tunnel, open Monday through Friday), the adverb does not (we drove through, let me through), the particle binds to the verb and can be separated from it (read it through, see it through, think this through), and the predicate adjective means finished (Are you through?, I'm through with him). The path sense (through the tunnel) belongs with the movement prepositions.
entries.variants: thru (informal American spelling; signage, menus, and drive-thru — never in edited prose)
entries.see also: inclusive, ago, pending, beginning, up to, as of, until
